### ## Who Governs Canada’s Protected and Conserved Areas?

**Governance** describes who holds authority and responsibility for a specific protected or conserved area.It is important to understand that governance of land and ocean area in Canada is complex. While the federal government, along with Indigenous Nations, have primary jurisdiction over management decisions in the ocean, provincial and territorial governments have primary jurisdiction over land, most freshwater, and associated natural resources. In fact, federal lands account for only 6% of Canada’s landmass, while 76% are provincial and territorial, 6% are Indigenous owned, and 12% are under private ownership (ECCC, 2024b). Furthermore, Indigenous Peoples’ rights apply across all land and ocean territory in Canada and the status of treaties between Indigenous nations and federal, provincial, and territorial governments varies in different regions ([**Chapter****6**](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/pcacanadaen/chapter/ipcas/)). As such, federal actions will not work on their own to achieve area-based conservation goals. In addition, provincial, territorial, and Indigenous leadership will be essential.

While many people think that PCAs must be designated and managed by governments, that is not the case. International guidance is clear that PCAs can be governed by government or non-government organizations or can be jointly governed. Both protected areas and OECMs fall within a spectrum of governance types recognized by the IUCN (Dudley, 2013), including (see also **Figure****1.****9**):

**Governance by governments:** In the Canadian context, this could include federal, provincial, territorial, and municipal government protected areas, for example many national and provincial parks and protected areas.

**Shared governance:** This could include combinations of governments and NGOs. Shared governance typically refers to a collaboration between government agencies (federal, provincial, or territorial governments) and other parties (Indigenous Peoples, a municipality, a property owner, or a land trust), in which partners share the authority by making decisions collectively.

**Private governance:** Privately protected areas could be under the control of individual landowners, NGOs, corporations, or other private entities. Permanently protected lands on private land held by land trusts such as the Nature Conservancy of Canada would be in this category.

**Governance by Indigenous Peoples and local communities:** This could include areas governed by Indigenous nations, organizations, and/or communities. These areas can encompass a variety of land protection initiatives including Tribal Parks, Indigenous Cultural Landscapes, and Indigenous PCAs.

A large majority (nearly 77%) of reported PCAs are governed by provincial, territorial, or federal governments when we consider sites by _area_ (**Figure****1.****10**). Of this:

Provincial and territorial governments administer or jointly administer approximately 66% (905,595 km 2) of terrestrial protected and conserved area, and 2.8% (23,721 km 2) of marine protected and conserved area.

The federal government administers or jointly administers 34.6% (473,411 km 2) of terrestrial protected and conserved area. Of this, Parks Canada (responsible for national parks and national park reserves) administers 26% of protected and conserved areas, and Environment and Climate Change Canada administer 6% (through National Wildlife Areas (NWAs) and Migratory Bird Sanctuaries (MBSs). Other federal agencies (e.g., the National Capital Commission and Department of National Defense) make up the remaining 3% of the system.

The federal government also administers or jointly administers 98.6% (831,427 km 2) of marine protected and conserved area (note: due to rounding/corrections in data totals do not add up to 100%).

Canada’s marine PCAs are managed almost entirely by three federal departments: 1) Fisheries and Oceans Canada (79%) (in the form of Marine Protected Areas (MPAs)) and marine refuges (OECMs); 2) Parks Canada (14%) (mostly in the form of National Marine Conservation Areas (NMCAs)); and Environment and Climate Change Canada (almost 4%, in National Wildlife Areas (NWAs) and Migratory Bird Sanctuaries (MBSs)). About 3% of the areas are managed provincially (and mostly in Nunavut, Québec, and B.C.).

Over 22% of terrestrial and marine protected and conserved area across six provinces and three territories are administered through shared governance arrangements, while private governance makes up only 0.4% of such area. While 0.4% may appear small relative to other governance types, privately protected and conserved areas are found almost exclusively in southern Canada and often protect sensitive and significant natural habitat in highly developed landscapes. There are about 150 land trusts working to protect private land across Canada at the local, provincial and national levels. The [Nature Conservancy of Canada (NCC)](https://www.natureconservancy.ca/en/?_ga=2.82723348.384016202.1745838330-1756080132.1745838330), Canada’s largest land trust, has partnered with individuals, organizations, and governments to conserve land across the country.Other organizations, like the [BC Parks Foundation](https://bcparksfoundation.ca/) and the [Nova Scotia Nature Trust](https://nsnt.ca/) work at the provincial scale, while local land trusts like [Action Chelsea for Respect of the Environment (ACRE)](https://acrechelsea.qc.ca/en) in Québec are working at the community level. These organizations rely on donations, government support, fundraising campaigns, and/or partnerships to support their conservation efforts.

# **Canada’s****P****rotected and****C****onserved****A****rea****s****with a****F****ocus on Recent Trends and Influences**

In recent years, significant progress has been made in establishing new PCAs, particularly in the marine environment, with many more sites currently being proposed and negotiated. While a comprehensive history of protected and conserved area establishment in Canada is beyond the scope of this chapter, several transformative changes are worth noting, including more inclusive approaches to conservation and unprecedented federal investments to support a broad suite of PCA initiatives across the country.

The accelerated progress achieved over the past decade was triggered by a 2015 political commitment by the federal government to deliver on the target to protect at least 17% of land and 10% of ocean by 2020. This commitment, made in response to sustained efforts by conservation NGOs, sparked a new spirit of cooperation among Crown governments, Indigenous nations and communities, and other partners to expand protection of Canada’s land and ocean.

The proportion of ocean estate reported as protected rose quickly and dramatically from 2016 to 2020, led by the federal government, which has primary responsibility for ocean management. On land, provinces and territories have primary jurisdiction and the federal government recognized that a collaborative pan-Canadian approach was needed with a new process called the **Pathway to Canada Target 1**. This in turn led to a public commitment in 2017 from Ministers responsible for parks and protected areas in federal, provincial, and territorial governments to work together with Indigenous governments, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), industry stakeholders, and the Canadian public to develop a pathway to achieve the 2020 terrestrial target and set the stage for completing an effective network of protected areas beyond 2020. While Québec is not a participant in the p athway process,the province has a parallel process for delivering on the international protected and conserved area targets.

Federal, provincial, and territorial governments also produced a report called, _One with Nature_, that outlines a pan-Canadian framework and approach for establishing a network of protected and conserved areas that recognizes protected areas and OECMs (as defined by IUCN), including those under Indigenous governance (Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas or IPCAs), all contributing to achieving Canada’s protected and conserved area targets (Government of Canada, 2018).

An integral part of the Pathway to Canada Target 1 process was the creation of an **Indigenous Circle of Experts****(ICE)**and a **National Advisory Panel** to advise Ministers on implementing the target. Both these advisory groups produced reports with recommendations focused in large part on the need to proceed in full partnership with Indigenous nations and communities, guided by both Indigenous knowledge and science. The National Advisory Panel included Indigenous and non-Indigenous appointees from Indigenous communities, NGOs, academia, and industry perspectives, all with significant conservation-related expertise. The resulting report, _Canada’s Conservation Vision_, includes 38 recommendations focused on issues such as governance, reconciliation, quality and standards, and investment (National Advisory Panel, 2018). The landmark ICE report, _We Rise Together_, resulted from extensive consultation with Indigenous communities and leaders. The report emphasizes the essential role of Indigenous leadership in achieving effective conservation and recognizes Indigenous communities’ stewardship of Canada’s landscapes for millennia, rooted in traditional knowledge. It also outlines recommendations for integrating Indigenous knowledge into the management of PCAs across Canada (ICE, 2018) (**Box****1.****4**).

The concept of ethical space was central to all this pathway work. **Ethical space** is defined as follows:

“_T_ _h_ _e_ _‘_ _ethical space_ _’_ _is formed when two societies, with disparate world views, are poised to engage each other. It is the thought about diverse societies_ _a_ _n_ _d_ _the space between them that contributes to the development of a framework for dialogue between human communities_ _”_ (Ermine, 2007, p. 193).

In the pathway context, ethical space is about ensuring that Indigenous knowledge systems and western science approaches are respected as equal and valid. The pathway process, and particularly the ICE, has spurred an important and transformational shift towards greater recognition and commitment to reconciliation and Indigenous rights in conservation, exemplified by the [UN _Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples_](https://www.un.org/development/desa/indigenouspeoples/wp-content/uploads/sites/19/2018/11/UNDRIP_E_web.pdf) (UNDRIP) and the [Truth and Reconciliation Commission](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1450124405592/1529106060525), as well as in efforts to meet international biodiversity conservation targets (Mansuy et al., 2023; Townsend et al., 2020; Zurba et al., 2019).

**B****OX****1.****4****.****What are****Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas****?**

While the term _Indigenous Protected and Conserved_ _Area_ (IPCA) is new, the concept is not. IPCAs have emerged as a vital form of area-based conservation in Canada. There is no strict definition of what constitutes an IPCA, as this will depend on the partners involved in creating, governing, and managing an area. While IPCAs can vary in terms of their governance and management objectives, they generally share three essential elements:

**[![Image 14: Front cover of the report We Rise Together: Achieving Pathway to Canada Target 1 through the creation of Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas. Photograph shows members of the Indigenous Circle of Experts and participants at the Northern Regional Gathering on Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs) at Aurora Village, Yellowknife, NWT.](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/app/uploads/sites/6495/2025/10/ReportCover-232x300.jpg)](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/app/uploads/sites/6495/2025/10/ReportCover-scaled.jpg)1. IPCAs are Indigenous-led.** Indigenous Peoples have the primary role in determining objectives, boundaries, management plans, and governance structures for IPCAs. This is part of their exercise of self-determination;

**2. IPCAs involve a long-term commitment to the conservation of lands and waters for future generations**; and,

**3. IPCAs highlight Indigenous rights and responsibilities.** An example is the responsibility to care for, and respect, lands and waters consistent with natural and Indigenous laws.

_(_ _ICE_ _,_ _2018)_

The ICE report advocates for empowering Indigenous Peoples as leaders in conservation through the establishment of IPCAs. It also stresses the importance of legal recognition and support from Canadian governments for IPCAs, ensuring Indigenous communities have the authority and resources to govern these lands and waters effectively.

The recommendations from the ICE report have fostered greater recognition of Indigenous leadership and governance, and greater collaboration between Indigenous communities and Crown governments. The elevated recognition of Indigenous-led conservation efforts is already leading to significant conservation gains, including the establishment of Edehzhie Dehcho Protected Area and National Wildlife Area (14,218 km²) in the Northwest Territories, Thaidene Nëné Indigenous Protected Area (14,070 km²), and Kitaskino Nuwenëné Wildland Provincial Park in Alberta (3,145 km²). These efforts have contributed to restoring greater decision-making authority to Indigenous communities over their lands through co-governance and co-management of these protected areas. The financial support available in recent years for Indigenous-led conservation and stewardship initiatives is leading to a growing number of Indigenous-led conservation proposals from coast to coast to coast (Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society, 2022).

Political commitment to ambitious targets has led to unprecedented financial commitments for implementation from the Government of Canada. The 2018 federal budget included a historic investment of $1.35 billion over five years towards terrestrial nature conservation. At the time, this investment was the largest single conservation investment in Canadian history. It was also significant because it reached beyond the federal government to include significant support for conservation action by Indigenous nations and organizations, provincial and territorial governments, NGOs (including land trusts working on private land), and other partners. Moreover, it leveraged significant matching investments from philanthropic and other sources. This 2018 federal investment included over $118 million to support Indigenous-led conservation initiatives, including **Indigenous Guardians**and IPCAs.

An even bigger federal investment was announced in Budget 2021, tied to the updated targets of 25% protection by 2025 and 30% protection by 2030. This included $2.3 billion over five years for terrestrial conservation and $976.8 million over five years for marine conservation. Once again, significant portions were allocated to support partner actions, including $200 million for **Nature Agreements** with provincial and territorial governments, and $454 million for Indigenous-led conservation initiatives. An additional $800 million was announced at the UN Biodiversity Convention COP 15 in Montreal to support up to four Indigenous-led conservation initiatives with the potential to protect up to one million square kilometers (ECCC, 2022c).

In addition to expanding the coverage of PCAs, Target 3 of the UN CBD _Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework_ calls for more effective governance and inclusive management practices. Canada has responded by including quality-focused actions in **_Canada’s 2030 Nature Strategy_**, such as using KBAs to guide the identification and establishment of protected areas and establishing [Parks Canada’s National Program for Ecological Corridors](https://parks.canada.ca/nature/science/conservation/corridors-ecologiques-ecological-corridors). This focuses on efforts to enhance the connectivity between PCAs, allowing species to move and natural processes to flow freely across large landscapes (see [**Chapter****9**](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/pcacanadaen/chapter/climatechange/)) (Beazley et al., 2023).

Through these strategic investments and initiatives, the federal government has demonstrated a transformative commitment to expanding PCAs, marked by unprecedented collaborations with Indigenous communities, NGOs, and other stakeholders. While these efforts represent major steps forward towards Canada’s goal of protecting 30% of land and freshwater by 2030, much work remains. Moving forward, it will be important to continue to operate under the guiding pathway principles. It is also important to build upon the framework of the _One with Nature_ report and the recommendations of ICE’s _We Rise Together_ and _Canada’s Conservation Vision_ developed by the National Advisory Panel.

# **Conclusions:****Is Canada****Living Up to****i****ts****P****rotected and****C****onserved****A****rea****A****spirations****?**

As detailed in this chapter, Canada has taken significant steps to better align its conservation efforts, guided by evolving targets and frameworks established by the CBD and IUCN. Notable achievements include: 1) federal commitment and investments to deliver on ambitious targets; 2) commitments and actions to expand protected and conserved area systems by some provinces and territories (including Québec, British Columbia, Manitoba, Yukon, NWT, Nova Scotia); 3) greater recognition of and support for Indigenous-led conservation initiatives; and 4) the development of creative, knowledge-based, and forward-looking initiatives, such as the Pathway Initiative, and _Canada’s 2030_ _Nature_ _Strategy_. These developments reflect an evolving recognition of the urgent need to conserve biodiversity and its interdependence with human health and well-being (see [**Chapter 8**](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/pcacanadaen/chapter/health/)).

However, despite the growing international and national commitments and the expansion of PCAs across much of the country, wildlife and ecosystems continue to decline (WWF, 2024). While PCAs are without doubt an effective tool in the battle against biodiversity loss, gains in protected and conserved areas are being outpaced by resource development. Like many nations, Canada has prioritized development and resource use in most of its landscapes and seascapes, resulting in ongoing biodiversity loss. Independent audits over the past decade consistently show a significant gap between Canada’s PCA commitments and the outcomes achieved (Office of the Auditor General of Canada, 2018; Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, 2023). [**Chapter****s****2**](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/pcacanadaen/chapter/pcagovernance/) and [**3**](https://ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/pcacanadaen/chapter/terrestrial-freshwater/)explore these issues in greater depth. Recent NGO assessments have illustrated the inconsistencies between federal, provincial, and territorial government commitments and contributions to achieving the targets (CPAWS, 2025).

Yet Canada has one of the best opportunities in the world to deliver the scale of conservation action necessary to halt and reverse biodiversity loss. A report by the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (CPAWS, 2022) demonstrated that doubling the area of land and ocean protected by 2030 is realistic and possible if all relevant agencies and governance partners, including at the provincial and territorial level, demonstrate the necessary political will and financial investments to deliver. If the many opportunities outlined in this report were implemented, Canada would be on track to achieve its terrestrial and marine conservation targets.

There are only five years left to deliver on PCA commitments under the UN CBD _Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework_. Establishing new protected areas and recognizing new OECMs _takes time_, requiring trust-building among authorities, stakeholders, and rightsholders—efforts that also demand sustained investment. With federal funding commitments currently set to expire in early 2026—and limited willingness from some provinces and territories to contribute to achieving this target—there is an urgent need to renew both investment and commitment now. Canada must also work diligently to address the quality dimensions of Target 3, ensuring conservation effectiveness and ecological connectivity. Achieving this will require a **whole-of-society** and **whole-of-government** approach, such as through inclusive land and ocean spatial planning, monitoring and reporting outcomes, oversight, coherence, and meaningful engagement with rightsholders and stakeholders. It also requires better reflecting the benefits of conservation in decision-making and budgeting processes, including by assessing the enormous costs of inaction.

This will be no easy task. The remaining chapters in this textbook examine solutions to these challenges with the aim of equipping readers with the critical knowledge and analytical tools necessary to implement effective and equitable solutions that advance the ecological integrity, resilience, and inclusivity of PCAs in Canada, and in so doing, reversing the biodiversity loss that threatens our well-being and that of our children and grandchildren.

**An Indigenous Reflection on Protected and Conserved Areas: Part One**

When this textbook was conceived, a key goal was to meaningfully include Indigenous reflections on concepts often only presented from scientific or government perspectives. While many chapter author teams included Indigenous perspectives and case studies, co-editor Eli Enns has provided reflections on the theme of Protected and Conserved Areas in Canada: Advancing Policy, Practice,and Indigenous Leadership that are shared at the end of each chapter.

We invite readers to imagine Eli sharing his thoughts in the _Naa’waya’sum_ garden at the Clayoquot Campus of the Pacific [Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCA) Innovation Centre](https://ipcainnovation.ca/). Participants of programs at that site are usually invited to gather in a circle around the _Naa’was_ totem pole, which depicts—in general—the Tla-o-qui-aht first teachings of respect for all life and responsibilities to future generations. Eli or another teacher would share what they think we should know about the [_Tla-o-qui-aht_](https://www.tribalparks.com/)[Tribal Parks](https://www.tribalparks.com/)created in 1984 to protect old-growth forests from logging, about IPCAs, and about Indigenous ways of knowing and being.

# **Next Steps for Managers,****Policymakers****,****and Practitioners**

1.   **Mainstream a Whole-of-Society/Government Approach:**Achieving Canada’s 30×30 target requires unprecedented collaboration across governments, Indigenous Peoples and other rightsholders and stakeholders, and various influencing sectors (e.g., agriculture, forestry, energy, transportation). Governments must focus on both expanding and improving the quality, equity, and governance of protected areas, with continued support for Indigenous leadership.
2.   **Identify Priority Areas for Protection:**Urgent action is needed to address biodiversity loss and identify priority areas for protection amid population growth and development. Chapters 3 and 4 discuss methods for identifying protected areas in terrestrial and marine environments, respectively.
3.   **Increase Long-Term, Sustainable Funding:**Effective biodiversity conservation requires long-term financial investments. Despite unprecedented federal financial commitments to support area-based conservation, some provinces (notably Ontario, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Alberta) have not committed to expanded action and have made little progress. Sustained public funding is essential to encourage progress, leverage private and philanthropic investments, maintain momentum, enhance monitoring, and support Indigenous-led conservation initiatives and Indigenous Guardian programs.

definition

The variability among living organisms from all sources including, inter alia, terrestrial, marine, and other aquatic ecosystems and the ecological complexes of which they are part; this includes diversity within species, between species, and of ecosystems (CBD, 1992, Article 2).

×Close definition

A dynamic complex system of plant, animal, and micro-organism communities and their non-living environment interacting as a functional unit (CBD, 1992, Article 2).

×Close definition

Refers generally to actions taken to protect and manage specific geographic areas to conserve biodiversity and ecosystem services. These measures can include both protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs). Area-based conservation measures are considered essential for maintaining ecological integrity and supporting the sustainable use of natural resources.

×Close definition

A condition that is determined to be characteristic of its natural region and likely to persist, including abiotic components and the composition and abundance of native species and biological communities, rates of change, and supporting processes (Canada National Parks Act, 2000).

×Close definition

A clearly defined geographic space that is recognized, dedicated, and managed—by legal or other effective means—to ensure the long-term conservation of nature, along with its associated ecosystem services and cultural values (Dudley, 2013).

×Close definition

The conservation of ecosystems and natural habitats, and the maintenance and recovery of viable species populations in their natural environments. For domesticated or cultivated species, this refers to conserving them in the environments where they developed their unique characteristics (CBD, 1992, Article 2).

×Close definition

Contrasts with in-situ conservation and is conservation that occurs at zoos, aquaria, and botanical gardens.

×Close definition

A global organization that works to conserve nature and promote the sustainable use of natural resources. It is best known for the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species and for setting international standards for conservation and protected areas.

×Close definition

A specialist group within the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) that supports the establishment and effective management of protected and conserved areas worldwide. It brings together over 2,500 experts from around the globe to develop best practices, guidance, and policy advice for biodiversity conservation. The WCPA plays a key role in advancing global conservation targets, including those under the UN Convention on Biological Diversity.

×Close definition

A geographically defined area other than a protected area, which is governed and managed in ways that achieve positive and sustained long-term outcomes for the in situ conservation of biological diversity, with associated ecosystem functions and services and, where applicable, cultural, spiritual, socioeconomic, and other locally relevant values (CBD, 2018).

×Close definition

In the context of this textbook, PCAs refer to protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs). The term conserved area is increasingly used synonymously with OECMs.

×Close definition

Part of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework that calls on Parties to the CBD to: “Ensure and enable that by 2030 at least 30 per cent of terrestrial, inland water, and of coastal and marine areas, especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services, are effectively conserved and managed through ecologically representative, well-connected and equitably governed systems of protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures, recognizing indigenous and traditional territories where applicable, and integrated into wider landscapes, seascapes and the ocean, while ensuring that any sustainable use, where appropriate in such areas, is fully consistent with conservation outcomes, recognizing and respecting the rights of indigenous peoples and local communities, including over their traditional territories” (CBD, 2022, Target 3).

×Close definition

A historic agreement under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) that commits nations to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030. The framework, agreed to in 2022, supports the achievement of the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals and builds on the CBD’s previous Strategic Plans, setting out an ambitious pathway to reach the global vision of a world living in harmony with nature by 2050. Among the Framework’s key elements are 4 goals for 2050 and 23 targets for 2030.

×Close definition

See “Target 3”.

×Close definition

A government, regional authority, institution, individual, Indigenous community or organization, non-profit organization, corporation, municipality, regional county municipality, community group, or any other body recognized as having partial or complete powers and responsibilities in decision-making and management of an area. The central authorities accountable are entities responsible for decision-making on the site’s objectives and its day-to-day management (Government of Québec, 2024).

×Close definition

The official national source of spatial and attribute data on all marine and terrestrial protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs) in Canada. It also includes Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs) that meet Canadian criteria.

×Close definition

The concept of long-term is central to the definitions of both protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs). According to guidance from the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), "long-term" means that a site is expected to conserve biodiversity in perpetuity, rather than on a temporary or time-limited basis (Fitzsimons et al., 2024).

×Close definition

The benefits people obtain from ecosystems, which include supporting, regulating, provisioning, and cultural services.

×Close definition

Lands and waters where Indigenous governments have the primary role in protecting and conserving ecosystems through Indigenous laws, governance, and knowledge systems (Indigenous Circle of Experts, 2018).

×Close definition

Describes processes that are free from manipulation or coercion, informed by adequate and timely information, and occur sufficiently prior to a decision so that Indigenous rights and interests can be incorporated or addressed effectively as part of the decision-making process. The goal is to genuinely seek the consent of affected Indigenous Peoples. FPIC is about working together in partnership and respect (Canada Department of Justice, 2025).

×Close definition

Refers to all contributions—beneficial and detrimental—that people, individually or collectively at various scales, derive or endure from Nature.

×Close definition

The ability to understand how natural systems work, how human actions affect those systems, and how to make informed, responsible decisions that support environmental sustainability. As a key goal of environmental education, environmental literacy enables individuals to critically assess the complex relationships between human society, ecosystems, and the changing climate, ultimately fostering sustainable and responsible behaviours.

×Close definition

Broadly refers to actions that individuals take to minimize harm to the environment or actively restore it.

×Close definition

Sites contributing significantly to the global persistence of biodiversity in terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems. The Global Standard for the Identification of Key Biodiversity Areas sets out globally agreed criteria for the identification of KBAs worldwide.

×Close definition

A collaboration between federal, provincial, territorial, Indigenous, and local governments as well as environmental non-governmental organization partners. Its four collective priorities are to: 1) Expand the systems of federal, provincial, and territorial protected and conserved area, 2) Promote greater recognition and support for existing Indigenous rights, responsibilities, and priorities in conservation, 3) Maximize conservation outcomes, and 4) Build support and participation for conservation with a broader community.

×Close definition

A fully Indigenous-led advisory body established under Canada’s Pathway to Target 1 initiative, focused on guiding the creation and implementation of Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs) across Canada. Formed in early 2017 and active through 2018, the group produced the landmark We Rise Together report, containing 28 recommendations to empower Indigenous governance, conservation, and stewardship.

×Close definition

As part of the Pathway to Canada Target 1 process, the NAP was established to provide recommendations that reflect a broad range of perspectives, grounded in the best available science and traditional knowledge. Its purpose was to advise on how governments, non-governmental organizations, and Canadians could work together to achieve Canada Target 1 (now Target 3). In so doing, it created a coordinated and connected network of protected and conserved areas across the country, serving as a cornerstone of biodiversity conservation for future generations.

×Close definition

Creates a place for knowledge systems to interact with mutual respect, kindness, generosity, and other basic values and principles. All knowledge systems are considered equal; no single system has more weight or legitimacy than another

×Close definition

Indigenous-led conservation stewards who serve as the eyes, ears and boots on the ground of their traditional territories. These individuals embody both ancestral knowledge and modern scientific expertise to monitor, manage, and protect ecosystems, cultural sites, and natural resources in alignment with Indigenous laws, values, and responsibilities.

×Close definition

Collaborative conservation initiatives between the federal government and provincial/territorial governments, often including Indigenous governments, to achieve shared conservation goals. These agreements outline specific, mutually agreed-upon actions and financial commitments to protect and conserve nature, including protected areas, species at risk, and ecosystem health.

×Close definition

A nationally coordinated vision and action plan, co-developed through public, Indigenous, and stakeholder engagement. It aims to align federal efforts with the Convention on Biological Diversity’s (CBD) Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework’s 23 global biodiversity targets, particularly Target 3.

×Close definition

All sectors and groups within society are engaged in and support biodiversity conservation. This approach recognizes that tackling biodiversity loss requires collaboration and engagement at all levels, not just through government action, but also with non-state actors like businesses, civil society organizations, and local communities (including young people).

×Close definition

Is to act at all levels of governance (reflecting the principles of the ecosystem approach).

×Close definition

## Abstract

Canada has committed to protecting 30% of its land by 2030, yet existing protected areas cover only 12.4% of Canadian lands, which is insufficient to protect terrestrial biodiversity. In this study, we identified priority areas for biodiversity conservation in Canada, using data on 1506 species across nine taxonomic groups. We first evaluated the effectiveness of existing protected areas in conserving at-risk and other species. Then, we applied optimization algorithms to determine priority areas that could enhance the existing system. Our results reveal that over 90% of the species studied have less than 30% of their spatial distribution currently protected. To meet a constant conservation target of protecting at least 30% of the spatial distribution for all species, Canada would need to expand its protected area system by 16%–17% of its total land area, focusing on regions like Nunavut, Quebec, and the Northwest Territories. Alternatively, when using relative conservation targets based on species’ range sizes, Canada would need to prioritize expanding protected areas by 4.56%–5.46% of its land, with new areas primarily in Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec. Achieving these goals will require collaborative strategies that respect Indigenous rights and involve agreements with private landowners.

## Introduction

Protected areas (PAs) are a crucial component of strategies to alleviate the ongoing biodiversity crisis (Watson et al. 2014). Recognizing this, 196 countries including Canada agreed to the Kunming Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF) to conserve 30% of their land by 2030 (GBF 2022). More specifically, based on Target 1 of the KM-GBF, countries committed to conserving biodiversity in their spatial planning process and to bring the loss of areas with a high ecological value to zero by 2030. Target 3 of the KM-GBF urges countries to protect at least 30% of their natural habitats by 2030, using a network of well-governed conservation areas that respect Indigenous rights and ensure sustainable practices. Additionally, the KM-GBF urges implementation of actions to prevent human-induced extinctions, significantly reduce extinction risks, maintain and restore genetic diversity across species, and manage human–wildlife interactions to promote coexistence through both in situ and ex situ conservation and sustainable management practices.

Effectively implementing the KM-GBF in Canada is crucial, as the country frequently contributes to ecosystem services beyond its 7% share of global land area. This creates both an opportunity and a responsibility for Canada to lead in conservation efforts and outcomes (Coristine et al. 2019). Nevertheless, the existing PA system in Canada is inadequate for meeting the KM-GBF Targets. Despite recent progress in expanding the national PA system, PAs only cover 12.4% of the country (ECCC 2023). These areas are insufficient for protecting Canada's biodiversity and over 800 species that are identified by the federal government as at risk of extinction (SAR) (COSEWIC 2020). For example, Bolliger et al. (2020) found PAs in Canada protect an average of only 8.1% of SAR ranges. Lin et al. (2020) showed that less than 10% of priority stopover sites of migratory birds in North America are protected officially, and Hardouin and Hargreaves (2023) confirmed that current PAs only cover less than 7% of species at risk hotspots. In addition, Hardouin and Hargreaves (2023) found that a majority of nationally and globally endangered species in Canada have less than 10% of their ranges within PAs. Furthermore, Canada's PA system is least adequate in its most biodiverse areas at the southern border, which is where human populations are particularly high (Eckert et al. 2023). Thus, it is imperative that efforts to expand Canada's PA system must be designed to address current shortfalls as the country moves forward in its commitment to the KM-GBF.

Previous studies have identified priority areas for conservation in Canada among certain taxonomic groups and regions. For example, Stralberg et al. (2018) identified high priority areas for songbird species across Canada, while Lin et al. (2020) evaluated stopovers of migratory birds across North America. Proctor et al. (2022) assessed the most effective allocation of resources for habitat protection for at-risk species in Ontario, Canada. Eckert et al. (2023) undertook a prioritization analysis of land for conservation using Zonation 5 (Moilanen et al. 2022) for plants, mammals, birds, butterflies, amphibians, reptiles in Canada excluding farmlands and areas with higher human disturbance. However, such areas can play an important role in biodiversity conservation (Santos-Filho et al. 2012; Ricciardi et al. 2021; Riva and Fahrig 2022), despite higher potential barriers to conservation. More generally, traditionally underrepresented taxa such as lichens, mosses, and mollusks have not been evaluated in previous PA selection studies across Canada.

Here, we provide the most comprehensive prioritization of Canadian lands for biodiversity conservation to date. To achieve this, we used the spatial distribution layers of 48 amphibians, 48 reptiles, 161 mammals, 510 birds, 401 arthropods, 297 vascular plants, 15 lichens, 17 mosses, and 9 mollusks in Canada. After compiling spatial distribution data for each of these species, we assessed the performance of existing PAs by comparing the percentage of each species’ spatial distribution covered by protected areas to a suite of target thresholds. We then used a systematic conservation planning approach to identify priority areas for addressing target shortfalls. Since the identification of priority areas depends on the underlying objectives, we explored a range of scenarios, using a factorial design varying targets from 30% of spatial distribution to flexible targets based on spatial distribution size, and varying cost from area-equivalent costs to human footprint (Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021) as a measure of relative cost. Finally, we evaluated how expanding the existing protected area system to include the priority areas could improve conservation efforts across Canada. Our conclusions serve to help the Canadian and provincial/territorial governments and conservation practitioners working at local scales identify nationally important areas for conserving biodiversity.

## Materials and methods

### Study system

We used 1 km×1 km grid cells as planning units for the prioritization (_N_=9880 260) across Canada. Each planning unit corresponds to a distinct piece of land that may be considered for the establishment of protected areas. All species distribution data and current PA boundary data (ECCC 2023), provincial boundary (STATCAN 2016), human footprint data (Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021), and Indigenous Lands (Government of Canada 2017) were resampled and reprojected if necessary to match the spatial properties of the planning units to a 1 km 2 spatial grid.

We examined 1506 terrestrial species across nine taxonomic groups in Canada. To achieve this, we compiled data from several sources (Table S1). From these species’ distribution datasets, we included data that delimited the presence and absence of species in particular locations (e.g., range polygons) and, where available, continuous data that delineated the abundance or habitat suitability of species in particular locations (e.g., species distribution models). We applied thresholds to the continuous datasets to standardize data across taxa (see Table S1 for details).

Although the complete dataset of 1506 species represent only a small portion of the over 47 000 native species in Canada (CESCC 2022), it encompasses a reasonably representative sample of Canada's terrestrial biodiversity given the breadth of taxa included. When distribution data for SAR species (COSEWIC 2020) were available from other sources, such as the Area of Habitat (AOH) map (Proctor et al. 2022; Schuster et al. 2023), we prioritized these over range data (Bolliger et al. 2020). The AOH maps align species ranges with terrestrial land cover datasets and elevation data to more accurately define the species’ AOH (Brook et al. 2019; Schuster et al. 2023). For migratory bird species present in the eBird dataset, we accommodated their migratory habitat requirements by treating their migratory and resident distributions as separate features in the prioritization (Butchart et al. 2015). We accessed the eBird database ([www.ebird.org](http://www.ebird.org/)) through the ebirdst R package v2.2021.1 (Auer et al. 2020; Auer et al. 2023). All analyses were performed in the R statistical computing environment v4.3.2 (R Core Team 2023).

### Representation targets

Representation targets specify the minimum percentage of a species’ (or ecosystems’) distribution that should ideally be protected to safeguard their long-term persistence (Friedrichs et al. 2018; González-Fernández et al. 2022). Since it can be difficult to set targets that are both meaningful for informing policy and for reducing extinction risk (MacKinnon et al. 2015), we examined two approaches for setting targets. Specifically, the approaches involve setting targets as (i) a constant 30% of species range, informed by the more general goals of protecting an ecologically representative 30% of land area (GBF 2022); and (ii) a variable percentage of each species’ total distribution, setting higher percentages for species with smaller distributions (Rodrigues et al. 2004; Hanson et al. 2020). In the second approach, for the species with a spatial extent smaller than 1000 km 2, we considered a 100% target (8 amphibians, 26 arthropods, 307 birds, 7 mammals, 3 reptiles, 21 vascular plants). For the species with a spatial extent larger than 1000 000 km 2 we considered a target of 100 000 km 2 (17 amphibians, 181 arthropods, 753 birds, 80 mammals, 5 reptiles, 12 vascular plants), and for the species with an intermediate spatial extent (between 1000 and 250 000 km 2), we assigned targets by loglinearly interpolating between these spatial extent thresholds with 10% and 100% target thresholds and used the 10% target for the species with a range of up to 1000 000 km 2.

### Protected area assessment

To assess the performance of existing protected areas, we overlaid species’ distributions with protected areas and calculated the percentage of each species’ distribution that was covered by existing PAs. We then compared each species’ representation by existing PAs to its targets (computed using the two approaches described above). Additionally, we identified species that are entirely absent from the existing protected areas.

### Spatial prioritizations

We generated spatial prioritizations under four different scenarios (Table 1). These scenarios represent a factorial design to examine the influence of different effective target settings and costs associated with establishing protected areas. Specifically, the analysis involved identifying priority areas using (i) loglinear targets and equal planning unit costs, (ii) loglinear targets and the human footprint index(Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021) for planning unit costs, (iii) constant (30%) targets and equal planning unit costs, and (iv) constant (30%) targets and the human footprint index for planning unit costs. We used the human footprint index as a cost metric in some scenarios because it is a useful index to reflect the potential complexity of planning in landscapes that are heavily used by humans (Venter et al. 2016; Tapia-Armijos et al. 2017; Schuster et al. 2019 _a_; Hardouin and Hargreaves 2023). However, we acknowledge that it is not a complete representation of human impacts on landscapes (Nolte 2020; Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021). Across all scenarios, we generated prioritizations using the minimum set formulation of the PA selection problem (see Beyer et al. 2016 for mathematical formulation). Briefly, this formulation identifies the cheapest set of planning units needed to meet the species’ representation targets. To account for existing conservation efforts, we locked in planning units covered by existing protected areas (see Fig. S2 for additional counterfactual scenarios that did not lock in existing PAs). As research has suggested that Indigenous stewardship of their lands supports high biodiversity levels that are comparable to protected regions (Schuster et al. 2019 _b_), we reran separate scenarios in which we also locked in Indigenous lands in addition to current protected areas. This is meant to reflect effective Indigenous stewardship of biodiversity. However, this does not imply that national governments have the authority to count these lands toward their conservation targets. All prioritizations were generated to optimality using the prioritizr R package (Hanson et al. 2023) and Gurobi optimization software (Gurobi Optimization 2023).

## Results

### Performance of existing protected areas

On average, the percentage of spatial distribution located within current PAs is higher for terrestrial SAR species than non-SAR species, across all groups except reptiles (Fig. 1). Currently, Canada's PAs fail to reach our 30% coverage goal for 1405 species (93% of species in our dataset). This includes 375 SAR (87.6% of SAR in our analysis). For 1295 species (86% of species in our dataset), including 344 SAR, less than 20% of spatial distribution are protected and for 791 species (52.5%), including 229 SAR, less than 10% of spatial distribution are protected. Based on a constant 30% target, mosses and arthropods are the groups with the highest and lowest percentages of species protected in Canada (18% and 3%, respectively). However, based on loglinear targets, mammals are the group with the highest percentage of species protected (49%) and both mollusks and mosses have no species adequately protected (Fig. 1).

### Prioritization scenarios

Our prioritization scenarios suggest that between 455 191 and 1714 470 km 2 (4.56%–17.17% of Canada's lands) of new PA would be needed to meet our species-based targets, with the lower value being for the scenario where all planning units have the same costs and the target was loglinear, and the upper value being for the scenario where human footprint was used as a cost layer and 30% of the spatial distribution of all species were required to be selected (Fig. 2). These numbers changed to 384 987–1198 719 km 2 when we locked in Indigenous lands in addition to current protected areas (Fig. S3). The land requirements for the counterfactual scenario where protected areas could be swapped suggest that between 904 717 and 2824 082 km 2 lands were needed to protect the conservation features (Fig. S2), implying that some current areas in the PA network may have redundancy in the species that they protect.

In scenarios with 30% as a constant target for all species, Nunavut, Quebec, and Northwest Territories had the largest land areas selected including current and new PAs, even after locking in Indigenous lands. This result is due to the preponderance of wide-ranged species at higher latitude in Canada, including such as woodland caribou (_Rangifer tarandus_), wolverine (_Gulo gulo_), ermine (_Mustela erminea_), Old World swallowtail (_Papilio Machaon_), common redpoll (_Acanthis flammea_), and polar bumble bee (_Bombus polaris_). In scenarios with loglinear targets, British Columbia, Nunavut, and Quebec are the provinces with the highest selected lands as PAs regardless of including Indigenous lands in the solution or not. When Indigenous lands were not included, Nunavut and Quebec and Northwest Territories have the largest percentage of recommended new PA for a constant 30% target, while Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec are the provinces with the largest percentage of recommended new PA for loglinear targets. However, when Indigenous lands are included, Quebec, Ontario, and Alberta have the highest percentage of new protected areas for a constant 30% target, and British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec are the provinces with the highest percentages for the loglinear targets (Tables 2 and S3).

## Discussion

We used both species-based and a constant 30% targets to prioritize potential land area for conservation, based on Canada's commitment to protect a representative 30% of its terrestrial area. We assumed that by protecting 30% of the spatial distribution of its species, Canada would likely be achieving such representation. A gap analysis indicates that for around 93% of 1506 species investigated, less than 30% of their spatial distributions in Canada are adequately represented by protected areas. Furthermore, for around half of these species, less than 10% of their spatial distributions are within the current PAs. We also used a flexible targeting approach based on species’ range sizes. Our systematic conservation planning results indicated that, based on various metrics included in scenarios, an additional 4.56%–17.17% of Canada is needed to be protected to meet either flexible spatial distribution-based targets or 30% spatial distribution targets in Canada.

Our analysis revealed that while mammals, like many other taxa, are significantly underrepresented in current PAs, their representation is higher compared to other taxa. This result is consistent with previous studies that have globally confirmed the taxonomic bias toward mammals and birds in conservation (e.g., Titley et al. 2017). However, our study did not find a bias towards birds, possibly because we considered migratory birds as underrepresented if either their breeding or migratory habitats within Canada did not meet the defined conservation targets. Conversely, the current PA system appears to be least effective in protecting terrestrial reptiles, mollusks, vascular plants, and lichens. Fewer than 20% of species in these groups are adequately represented in current PAs. This is not surprising, as these taxa are often overlooked in conservation research (Donaldson et al. 2017) or management (Evans et al. 2016; Creighton and Bennett 2019; Mammola et al. 2020)

Although we expected a high percentage of priority areas to be located within British Columbia, Quebec, and Ontario, the provinces that host the highest number of species (Fig. S1), our results suggest that there can be some exceptions in this regard. Nunavut, which hosts fewer species than many other Canadian jurisdictions, was one of the two provinces with the highest percentage of newly added PAs when we used a constant 30% target and regardless of the cost type assigned to the planning units and even without locking in the current PAs (Table S2). This result likely emerges because there are some unique species or migratory cycle habitats that depend on these areas, such as long-tailed duck (_Clangula hyemalis_), buff-bellied pipit (_Anthus rubescens_), northern collared lemming (_Dicrostonyx groenlandicus_), and Old World swallowtail (_Papilio machaon_).

Considering relative targets for different species could result in PA system that are potentially more biologically meaningful and more feasible than fixed targets. When we assign a uniform representation target of 30% to all species, we may consider species with very limited spatial distribution to be well-represented, even if PA covers only 30% of their limited range. Conversely, the 30% target represents a vast land area for widespread Canadian species that can inhabit large swaths of northern regions.

Counterfactual scenarios suggest some redundancy in Canada's PA system (Fig. S2). For example, when we set conservation targets using a loglinear function, 16.35%–27.19% less total PA required compared to current conditions. However, we note that there are many reasons for establishing PAs beyond protecting species’ ranges or habitats (Neugarten et al. 2024), and we also note that managing current PAs may be much more efficient in general than establishing and then managing new ones (Adams et al. 2019). Thus, given Canada's general shortfall in PA coverage, we do not recommend removing areas from the current PA portfolio.

When Indigenous lands were locked-in in addition to the current protected areas, an additional 3.9%–12.0% of Canada are theoretically needed to be protected to meet either flexible or constant 30% spatial distribution targets in Canada. We note that it is inappropriate to include Indigenous sovereign lands as “protected” in Canada's national protected areas system. However, our result does suggest that mutually agreed partnerships could be an important way forward to improve biodiversity protection in Canada. An example of a program that helps to facilitate this is the Project Finance for Permanence Program, which facilitates public and private funding for establishing and sustaining Indigenous protected areas (Government of Canada 2024).

Our results also indicate that protecting some areas with high human footprint may be very important for an effective biodiversity conservation, as the proportion of increased protected areas in these regions was 1.8–10.3 times higher in comparison to the rest of the study area (Table S4). This result is not surprising because many species, including SAR species, can be present in the human-dominated regions (Allan et al. 2019; OMECP 2019). This is especially the case in Canada, where high biodiversity areas in the south often coincide with high human populations and land pressure (Coristine et al. 2019; Proctor et al. 2022).

Our results differ from the most recent national-scale prioritization by Eckert et al. (2023) in two main aspects. First, Eckert et al. (2023) found that in national scenarios, 65% of their studied species will meet the 30% protection goal, which is equivalent to around 2598 380 km 2. Our results however indicated that if we increase the PA system to 2.1–2.4 times its current size (equivalent to maximum 2957 024 km 2 in total), all the species considered in our analysis will have at least 30% of their spatial distribution protected. One possible reason for this discrepancy can be different species used in our study versus what was used in Eckert et al. (2023). In their study, the taxa with the highest number of features in prioritization were plants; however, in our study birds had the highest number of conservation features. Second, in two scenarios we assigned a higher cost to the planning units (pixels) with higher human disturbance/footprint, while in Eckert et al. (2023), agricultural and highly disturbed areas were excluded from the analysis. Another explanation could be the optimization algorithms used in two studies. While Eckert et al. (2023) used Zonation 5 (Moilanen et al. 2022), which uses an iterative algorithm based on marginal loss for identifying near-optimal solutions, we used integer programming techniques that guarantee optimality.

Economic cost and feasibility are increasingly recognized as crucial considerations in conservation (Joseph et al. 2009; Wilson et al. 2009). Such consideration can lead to more realistic solutions. For example, Schuster et al. (2019 _a_) found that although considering human disturbance in conservation planning may require increased total PA, for some species, like migratory species, it is an important consideration as these species depend on a combination of intact and disturbed areas. Similar to Schuster et al. (2019 _a_), our analysis found that to protect 30% of species range, scenarios with human disturbance as cost require 4.2%–5.3% greater area than scenarios assigning a similar cost value to all the planning units (Fig. 2).

Our datasets represent a large number of Canadian species (including all listed terrestrial SAR that have been mapped), but they do not represent all taxa and facets of biodiversity in Canada. There are therefore possibilities for future improvements. For example, Indigenous knowledge was not included in our species spatial distribution estimates, nor was detailed habitat information beyond land cover types in species distribution models. In some cases, like vascular plants, arthropods, and birds, the resolution of the raster layers was coarser than our planning unit's size, and were resampled to the same resolution as the planning units (Table S1). In addition, we only considered species ranges and AOH in the prioritization process; however, contributing population-related variables for all the species in the prioritization can result in more robust results.

It is also important to note that our prioritization does not reflect all of the values and rights that are important in the process of area-based biodiversity prioritization, especially at the finer scales where actual land-use decisions will be made. In particular, we have not included Indigenous rights and values. For actual protection decisions, a more comprehensive approach that is led or co-led by Indigenous partners would be necessary, given that Canada is composed of traditional Indigenous territories. We also note that in many cases, Indigenous-led protection may take quite different forms to the target-based protection that is the focus of Canada's government. In addition, in areas where remnant habitats are confined to small but vital areas (Riva and Fahrig 2022), it will be important to carefully evaluate cost tradeoffs (Proctor et al. 2022) and consider alternative options such as private land stewardship programs. Furthermore, it is worth noting that our prioritization does not advise on the management actions that may need to be implemented inside priority areas to effectively conserve biodiversity (e.g., habitat restoration, invasive species management) (Tallis et al. 2021; Salgado-Rojas et al. 2023). A more comprehensive approach may also need to address various additional ecological, biological, and human-related factors (Haines et al. 2012).

## Conclusions

Our results show that we need to add between 1594 843 and 1714 470 km 2 to our current PA system to protect 30% of the spatial distribution of 1506 species in Canada (including terrestrial species at risk and native species such as migratory and resident birds, mammals, reptile, amphibians, bumblebees and butterflies, vascular plants, lichens, mosses, and mollusks), This means that Canada needs to more than double our current PAs of 1242 554 km 2. Considering both biodiversity and feasibility, the largest area additions would be in Ontario, British Columbia, Quebec if relative targets for the study species were used, and Nunavut, Quebec, and Northwest Territories if a constant 30% target for all the study species were used (Fig. 2; Table 2).

Given the vast area requirements for meeting Canada's biodiversity commitments, the task of conserving Canada's biodiversity will likely require challenging decisions for which areas to protect. It will likely also require creative approaches for places where protection is logistically or politically impossible. Partnerships with Indigenous rights holders will be crucial to achieving the letter and spirit of Canada's biodiversity protection commitment (ECCC 2024). Agreements with private landowners, and even temporary protection areas (Wen et al. 2023), may also play important supporting roles. For example, northern Canada contains large, intact landscapes with generally fewer competing land uses than in the south but requires support for Indigenous leadership and collaboration. Expansion in southern Canada will also require support for Indigenous leadership and collaboration but may face more numerous land use conflicts. Agreements with private landowners and even temporary arrangements (where permanence is unfeasible) will thus be important for conservation in southern Canada's biodiversity hotspots.

The output of our study provides a large-scale baseline for these finer-scale next steps by identifying the areas with the highest priority for the conservation of both at-risk and native species.

#### Data Availability Statement

In this study, we used existing datasets and did not conduct any primary data collection. The Area of Habitat layers was derived from IUCN range maps, which are available through the IUCN website (The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, retrieved 19 March 2022 from[https://www.iucnredlist.org/en](https://www.iucnredlist.org/en)). The Area of Habitat layers (for mammals, amphibians, and reptiles), the bumble bees distribution layers (Liczner et al. 2023), the butterflies distribution layers (eButterfly 2023), as well as the boundaries of protected areas are uploaded and accessible via Open Science Framework (OSF) at [https://osf.io/nh2ae/?view_only=9a5cfe83dc35490da007a175b7d6f71e](https://osf.io/nh2ae/?view_only=9a5cfe83dc35490da007a175b7d6f71e).

All other data related to the species considered in this study are available online through the sources listed in Table S1. The Human Footprint data are available in Hirsh-Pearson et al. (2021), and the Indigenous lands boundaries are available using Government of Canada Open Data Portal (Aboriginal Lands of Canada Legislative Boundaries: [https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/522b07b9-78e2-4819-b736-ad9208eb1067](https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/522b07b9-78e2-4819-b736-ad9208eb1067)).

## Abstract

Canada has committed to protecting 30% of its land by 2030, yet existing protected areas cover only 12.4% of Canadian lands, which is insufficient to protect terrestrial biodiversity. In this study, we identified priority areas for biodiversity conservation in Canada, using data on 1506 species across nine taxonomic groups. We first evaluated the effectiveness of existing protected areas in conserving at-risk and other species. Then, we applied optimization algorithms to determine priority areas that could enhance the existing system. Our results reveal that over 90% of the species studied have less than 30% of their spatial distribution currently protected. To meet a constant conservation target of protecting at least 30% of the spatial distribution for all species, Canada would need to expand its protected area system by 16%–17% of its total land area, focusing on regions like Nunavut, Quebec, and the Northwest Territories. Alternatively, when using relative conservation targets based on species’ range sizes, Canada would need to prioritize expanding protected areas by 4.56%–5.46% of its land, with new areas primarily in Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec. Achieving these goals will require collaborative strategies that respect Indigenous rights and involve agreements with private landowners.

## Introduction

Protected areas (PAs) are a crucial component of strategies to alleviate the ongoing biodiversity crisis (Watson et al. 2014). Recognizing this, 196 countries including Canada agreed to the Kunming Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF) to conserve 30% of their land by 2030 (GBF 2022). More specifically, based on Target 1 of the KM-GBF, countries committed to conserving biodiversity in their spatial planning process and to bring the loss of areas with a high ecological value to zero by 2030. Target 3 of the KM-GBF urges countries to protect at least 30% of their natural habitats by 2030, using a network of well-governed conservation areas that respect Indigenous rights and ensure sustainable practices. Additionally, the KM-GBF urges implementation of actions to prevent human-induced extinctions, significantly reduce extinction risks, maintain and restore genetic diversity across species, and manage human–wildlife interactions to promote coexistence through both in situ and ex situ conservation and sustainable management practices.

Effectively implementing the KM-GBF in Canada is crucial, as the country frequently contributes to ecosystem services beyond its 7% share of global land area. This creates both an opportunity and a responsibility for Canada to lead in conservation efforts and outcomes (Coristine et al. 2019). Nevertheless, the existing PA system in Canada is inadequate for meeting the KM-GBF Targets. Despite recent progress in expanding the national PA system, PAs only cover 12.4% of the country (ECCC 2023). These areas are insufficient for protecting Canada's biodiversity and over 800 species that are identified by the federal government as at risk of extinction (SAR) (COSEWIC 2020). For example, Bolliger et al. (2020) found PAs in Canada protect an average of only 8.1% of SAR ranges. Lin et al. (2020) showed that less than 10% of priority stopover sites of migratory birds in North America are protected officially, and Hardouin and Hargreaves (2023) confirmed that current PAs only cover less than 7% of species at risk hotspots. In addition, Hardouin and Hargreaves (2023) found that a majority of nationally and globally endangered species in Canada have less than 10% of their ranges within PAs. Furthermore, Canada's PA system is least adequate in its most biodiverse areas at the southern border, which is where human populations are particularly high (Eckert et al. 2023). Thus, it is imperative that efforts to expand Canada's PA system must be designed to address current shortfalls as the country moves forward in its commitment to the KM-GBF.

Previous studies have identified priority areas for conservation in Canada among certain taxonomic groups and regions. For example, Stralberg et al. (2018) identified high priority areas for songbird species across Canada, while Lin et al. (2020) evaluated stopovers of migratory birds across North America. Proctor et al. (2022) assessed the most effective allocation of resources for habitat protection for at-risk species in Ontario, Canada. Eckert et al. (2023) undertook a prioritization analysis of land for conservation using Zonation 5 (Moilanen et al. 2022) for plants, mammals, birds, butterflies, amphibians, reptiles in Canada excluding farmlands and areas with higher human disturbance. However, such areas can play an important role in biodiversity conservation (Santos-Filho et al. 2012; Ricciardi et al. 2021; Riva and Fahrig 2022), despite higher potential barriers to conservation. More generally, traditionally underrepresented taxa such as lichens, mosses, and mollusks have not been evaluated in previous PA selection studies across Canada.

Here, we provide the most comprehensive prioritization of Canadian lands for biodiversity conservation to date. To achieve this, we used the spatial distribution layers of 48 amphibians, 48 reptiles, 161 mammals, 510 birds, 401 arthropods, 297 vascular plants, 15 lichens, 17 mosses, and 9 mollusks in Canada. After compiling spatial distribution data for each of these species, we assessed the performance of existing PAs by comparing the percentage of each species’ spatial distribution covered by protected areas to a suite of target thresholds. We then used a systematic conservation planning approach to identify priority areas for addressing target shortfalls. Since the identification of priority areas depends on the underlying objectives, we explored a range of scenarios, using a factorial design varying targets from 30% of spatial distribution to flexible targets based on spatial distribution size, and varying cost from area-equivalent costs to human footprint (Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021) as a measure of relative cost. Finally, we evaluated how expanding the existing protected area system to include the priority areas could improve conservation efforts across Canada. Our conclusions serve to help the Canadian and provincial/territorial governments and conservation practitioners working at local scales identify nationally important areas for conserving biodiversity.

## Materials and methods

### Study system

We used 1 km×1 km grid cells as planning units for the prioritization (_N_=9880 260) across Canada. Each planning unit corresponds to a distinct piece of land that may be considered for the establishment of protected areas. All species distribution data and current PA boundary data (ECCC 2023), provincial boundary (STATCAN 2016), human footprint data (Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021), and Indigenous Lands (Government of Canada 2017) were resampled and reprojected if necessary to match the spatial properties of the planning units to a 1 km 2 spatial grid.

We examined 1506 terrestrial species across nine taxonomic groups in Canada. To achieve this, we compiled data from several sources (Table S1). From these species’ distribution datasets, we included data that delimited the presence and absence of species in particular locations (e.g., range polygons) and, where available, continuous data that delineated the abundance or habitat suitability of species in particular locations (e.g., species distribution models). We applied thresholds to the continuous datasets to standardize data across taxa (see Table S1 for details).

Although the complete dataset of 1506 species represent only a small portion of the over 47 000 native species in Canada (CESCC 2022), it encompasses a reasonably representative sample of Canada's terrestrial biodiversity given the breadth of taxa included. When distribution data for SAR species (COSEWIC 2020) were available from other sources, such as the Area of Habitat (AOH) map (Proctor et al. 2022; Schuster et al. 2023), we prioritized these over range data (Bolliger et al. 2020). The AOH maps align species ranges with terrestrial land cover datasets and elevation data to more accurately define the species’ AOH (Brook et al. 2019; Schuster et al. 2023). For migratory bird species present in the eBird dataset, we accommodated their migratory habitat requirements by treating their migratory and resident distributions as separate features in the prioritization (Butchart et al. 2015). We accessed the eBird database ([www.ebird.org](http://www.ebird.org/)) through the ebirdst R package v2.2021.1 (Auer et al. 2020; Auer et al. 2023). All analyses were performed in the R statistical computing environment v4.3.2 (R Core Team 2023).

### Representation targets

Representation targets specify the minimum percentage of a species’ (or ecosystems’) distribution that should ideally be protected to safeguard their long-term persistence (Friedrichs et al. 2018; González-Fernández et al. 2022). Since it can be difficult to set targets that are both meaningful for informing policy and for reducing extinction risk (MacKinnon et al. 2015), we examined two approaches for setting targets. Specifically, the approaches involve setting targets as (i) a constant 30% of species range, informed by the more general goals of protecting an ecologically representative 30% of land area (GBF 2022); and (ii) a variable percentage of each species’ total distribution, setting higher percentages for species with smaller distributions (Rodrigues et al. 2004; Hanson et al. 2020). In the second approach, for the species with a spatial extent smaller than 1000 km 2, we considered a 100% target (8 amphibians, 26 arthropods, 307 birds, 7 mammals, 3 reptiles, 21 vascular plants). For the species with a spatial extent larger than 1000 000 km 2 we considered a target of 100 000 km 2 (17 amphibians, 181 arthropods, 753 birds, 80 mammals, 5 reptiles, 12 vascular plants), and for the species with an intermediate spatial extent (between 1000 and 250 000 km 2), we assigned targets by loglinearly interpolating between these spatial extent thresholds with 10% and 100% target thresholds and used the 10% target for the species with a range of up to 1000 000 km 2.

### Protected area assessment

To assess the performance of existing protected areas, we overlaid species’ distributions with protected areas and calculated the percentage of each species’ distribution that was covered by existing PAs. We then compared each species’ representation by existing PAs to its targets (computed using the two approaches described above). Additionally, we identified species that are entirely absent from the existing protected areas.

### Spatial prioritizations

We generated spatial prioritizations under four different scenarios (Table 1). These scenarios represent a factorial design to examine the influence of different effective target settings and costs associated with establishing protected areas. Specifically, the analysis involved identifying priority areas using (i) loglinear targets and equal planning unit costs, (ii) loglinear targets and the human footprint index(Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021) for planning unit costs, (iii) constant (30%) targets and equal planning unit costs, and (iv) constant (30%) targets and the human footprint index for planning unit costs. We used the human footprint index as a cost metric in some scenarios because it is a useful index to reflect the potential complexity of planning in landscapes that are heavily used by humans (Venter et al. 2016; Tapia-Armijos et al. 2017; Schuster et al. 2019 _a_; Hardouin and Hargreaves 2023). However, we acknowledge that it is not a complete representation of human impacts on landscapes (Nolte 2020; Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021). Across all scenarios, we generated prioritizations using the minimum set formulation of the PA selection problem (see Beyer et al. 2016 for mathematical formulation). Briefly, this formulation identifies the cheapest set of planning units needed to meet the species’ representation targets. To account for existing conservation efforts, we locked in planning units covered by existing protected areas (see Fig. S2 for additional counterfactual scenarios that did not lock in existing PAs). As research has suggested that Indigenous stewardship of their lands supports high biodiversity levels that are comparable to protected regions (Schuster et al. 2019 _b_), we reran separate scenarios in which we also locked in Indigenous lands in addition to current protected areas. This is meant to reflect effective Indigenous stewardship of biodiversity. However, this does not imply that national governments have the authority to count these lands toward their conservation targets. All prioritizations were generated to optimality using the prioritizr R package (Hanson et al. 2023) and Gurobi optimization software (Gurobi Optimization 2023).

## Results

### Performance of existing protected areas

On average, the percentage of spatial distribution located within current PAs is higher for terrestrial SAR species than non-SAR species, across all groups except reptiles (Fig. 1). Currently, Canada's PAs fail to reach our 30% coverage goal for 1405 species (93% of species in our dataset). This includes 375 SAR (87.6% of SAR in our analysis). For 1295 species (86% of species in our dataset), including 344 SAR, less than 20% of spatial distribution are protected and for 791 species (52.5%), including 229 SAR, less than 10% of spatial distribution are protected. Based on a constant 30% target, mosses and arthropods are the groups with the highest and lowest percentages of species protected in Canada (18% and 3%, respectively). However, based on loglinear targets, mammals are the group with the highest percentage of species protected (49%) and both mollusks and mosses have no species adequately protected (Fig. 1).

### Prioritization scenarios

Our prioritization scenarios suggest that between 455 191 and 1714 470 km 2 (4.56%–17.17% of Canada's lands) of new PA would be needed to meet our species-based targets, with the lower value being for the scenario where all planning units have the same costs and the target was loglinear, and the upper value being for the scenario where human footprint was used as a cost layer and 30% of the spatial distribution of all species were required to be selected (Fig. 2). These numbers changed to 384 987–1198 719 km 2 when we locked in Indigenous lands in addition to current protected areas (Fig. S3). The land requirements for the counterfactual scenario where protected areas could be swapped suggest that between 904 717 and 2824 082 km 2 lands were needed to protect the conservation features (Fig. S2), implying that some current areas in the PA network may have redundancy in the species that they protect.
