About the indicators  

## About the indicators

### What the indicators measure

These indicators report the amount and proportion of Canada’s terrestrial (land and freshwater) and marine area that is recognized as conserved. Conserved areas are lands and waters which are managed in ways that achieve positive long-term outcomes for the conservation of biodiversity. They include protected areas as well as other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs). Canada recognizes the international definitions of protected areas and OECMs ([One with Nature](https://publications.gc.ca/site/eng/9.857393/publication.html)and [Guidance for recognizing marine Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/publications/oecm-amcepz/guidance-directives-2022-eng.html)) and implements the federal [Marine Protected Areas Protection Standard](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/mpa-zpm/protection-standard-norme-protection-eng.html) and [Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (OECM) Protection Standard](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/oecm-amcepz/protection-standard-norme-protection-eng.html).

Land and/or water access and use within protected areas are controlled primarily for the purpose of conserving nature (for example, a park, a conservation area or a wildlife reserve). OECMs are likewise managed over the long term in ways that result in the effective conservation of biodiversity, but they are not protected areas.

### Why these indicators are important

Well-managed conserved areas are one way to ensure the long-term persistence of populations of wild species and their habitats. Habitat conservation is a response to the loss of biodiversity and natural habitat. As the area conserved in Canada increases, more lands and waters are withdrawn from direct land development, thereby contributing to biodiversity conservation and improving the health of ecosystems. In turn, healthy ecosystems provide benefits such as clean water, mitigation of climate change, pollination and improved human health.

### Related initiatives

These indicators are used for reporting on the following [2022 to 2026 Federal Sustainable Development Strategy](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/climate-change/federal-sustainable-development-strategy.html) targets:

*   Conserve 25% of marine and coastal areas by 2025, and 30% by 2030, in support of the commitment to work to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030 in Canada, and achieve a full recovery for nature by 2050. The most recent data available shows that, as of the end of 2025, 15.5% of Canada’s coastal and marine areas was recognized as conserved through marine protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures, including 11.4% in protected areas
*   Conserve 25% of Canada’s land and inland waters by 2025, working toward 30% by 2030, from 12.7% recognized as conserved as of the end of 2020, in support of the commitment to work to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030 in Canada, and achieve a full recovery for nature by 2050. The most recent data available shows that, as of the end of 2025, 14.0% of Canada’s terrestrial areas and inland water was recognized as conserved through a network of protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures, including 12.9% in protected areas

The indicators are also used for reporting on Target 3 of [Canada’s 2030 Nature Strategy](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/biodiversity/canada-2030-nature-strategy.html): "Protected and conserved areas (30x30)." This target is related to the [Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework](https://www.cbd.int/article/cop15-final-text-kunming-montreal-gbf-221222) Target 3: "Ensure and enable that by 2030 at least 30 per cent of terrestrial, inland water, and of coastal and marine areas, especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services, are effectively conserved and managed through ecologically representative, well-connected and equitably governed systems of protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures, recognizing Indigenous and traditional territories, where applicable, and integrated into wider landscapes, seascapes and the ocean, while ensuring that any sustainable use, where appropriate in such areas, is fully consistent with conservation outcomes, recognizing and respecting the rights of Indigenous peoples and local communities including over their traditional territories."

In addition, the indicators contribute to the [Sustainable Development Goals of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development](http://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/). They are linked to Goal 14, Life Below Water and Target 14.5, "By 2020, conserve at least 10% of coastal and marine areas, consistent with national and international law and based on the best available scientific information." They are also linked to Goal 15, Life on Land and Target 15.1, "By 2020, ensure the conservation, restoration and sustainable use of terrestrial and inland freshwater ecosystems and their services, in particular forests, wetlands, mountains and drylands, in line with obligations under international agreements."

### Related indicators

The [Ability of the agricultural landscape to support wildlife](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/environmental-indicators/agricultural-landscape-support-wildlife.html) indicator provides a measure of the suitability of agricultural land as habitat for terrestrial vertebrates.

The [Ecological integrity of national parks](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/environmental-indicators/ecological-integrity-national-parks.html) indicator reports on the condition of ecosystems within national parks, an important element of Canada’s conserved area network.

The [Extent of Canada's wetlands](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/environmental-indicators/extent-wetlands.html) indicator reports the current known extent or area of land in Canada covered by wetlands at the national level, as well as by ecozones and ecoregions.

The [Global trends in conserved areas](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/environmental-indicators/global-trends-conserved-areas.html) indicator compares Canada’s conserved area to a peer group of countries.

Data sources and methods

## Data sources and methods

### Data sources

Data are taken from the [Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-wildlife-areas/protected-conserved-areas-database.html) (CPCAD).Data from federal, provincial and territorial governments, Indigenous governments, local governments, non-governmental organizations, and private landowners, are compiled by Environment and Climate Change Canada.

More information

### Protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures

Conserved areas are comprised of protected areas and other area-based conservation measures (OECMs).

Protected areas are areas recognized as meeting the [international definition](https://portals.iucn.org/library/node/30018) for a protected area as defined by the International Union for Conservation of Nature: "a clearly defined geographical space, recognised, dedicated and managed, through legal or other effective means, to achieve the long-term conservation of nature with associated ecosystem services and cultural values."

Other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs) are areas recognized as meeting the Convention on Biodiversity definition: "a geographically defined area other than a Protected Area, which is governed and managed in ways that achieve positive and sustained long-term outcomes for the in-situ conservation of biodiversity."Footnote 8Canada implements the Convention on Biodiversity’s OECM definition in a manner that reflects national circumstances. Guidance for assessing sites as Protected Areas or OECMs in Canada is provided through the Pathway to Canada Target 1 Decision Support Tool.Footnote 9 Guidance for assessing federal marine OECMs is provided through the [Marine OECM guidance](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/publications/oecm-amcepz/guidance-directives-2022-eng.html).

In Canada, Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Parks Canada and Environment and Climate Change Canada each have specific but complementary mandates for establishing marine protected areas:

*   [Oceans Act Marine Protected Areas](http://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/mpa-zpm/index-eng.html) (Fisheries and Oceans Canada) are parts of the ocean that are legally protected and managed to achieve the long-term conservation of nature. This can include protecting species that are fished, endangered or threatened marine species, as well as unique habitats and areas of high biological productivity or biodiversity
*   [National marine conservation areas](https://www.pc.gc.ca/en/amnc-nmca) (Parks Canada) are established to conserve representative examples of Canada’s natural and cultural marine heritage and to provide opportunities for public education and enjoyment
*   [National wildlife areas](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-wildlife-areas.html) (Environment and Climate Change Canada) are established and managed to conserve habitat for the recovery of species at risk and the conservation of migratory birds. Similarly, [migratory bird sanctuaries](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/migratory-bird-sanctuaries/locations.html) are managed to support the conservation of migratory birds through the regulation of hunting and activities that might affect habitat

The areas established by these departments, along with provincially and terrestrially established areas, contribute to the [conservation network](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/networks-reseaux/index-eng.html). The primary goal of this network is to provide long-term conservation of marine biodiversity, ecosystem function and special natural features.

Different organizations conserve areas for different purposes,Footnote 10and control the amount of human activity (such as transportation, fishing or recreation) that is allowed. Marine conservation efforts include a wide range of management and stewardship activities. Examples include support for the recovery of species at risk, prevention and mitigation of the impact of aquatic invasive species, and strengthening of Canada’s response to ship-source marine pollution.

### Data description

CPCAD contains data consolidated from various reporting authorities including federal, provincial, and territorial governments, Indigenous governments, local governments, non-governmental organizations, and private landowners. Once each year, these data providers submit geospatial and ancillary data for conserved areas under their administrative control. Data is current as of December 31, 2025.

The data include the name of the area, its geospatial location, boundaries, official area, biome (terrestrial/marine), International Union for Conservation of Nature management category, managing jurisdiction, and protection date,Footnote 11among other information.

In cases where the same attribute information does not apply to the entire conserved area, the area is divided into zones for reporting. For example, a single protected area that crosses a provincial border is divided into zones corresponding to the different provinces. Similarly, a protected area that is later expanded is treated as several zones, each with its own protection date. Terrestrial and marine sections are treated as separate zones; freshwater is included in the terrestrial zone. Supporting data are maintained independently for each zone. Conserved areas that are undivided are treated as a single zone.

Work is ongoing to capture and incorporate data on additional privately held protected areas and on areas being conserved through means other than formal [protection](https://portals.iucn.org/library/node/30018).

### Methods

The area conserved is estimated by means of a geographical analysis based on reported boundaries, accounting for overlaps. Separate estimates are made for protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs).

More information

#### Calculating Canada's conserved area

The [Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-wildlife-areas/protected-conserved-areas-database.html) (CPCAD) contains information on the protection (or conservation) date for each zone. For zones that have been delisted, the records are transferred to the Delisted database.

To estimate the terrestrial protected area trend over time:

1.   All polygons representing terrestrial protected areas that were protected in 1990 or earlier were selected from the database
2.   The selected polygons were dissolved into a single polygon (removing overlaps), and the resulting area calculated using Albers Equal Area Conic projection
3.   The process was repeated for each subsequent year (delisted areas were removed from the analysis starting in the year they were delisted)
4.   Estimates were divided by the total terrestrial area of Canada to determine the proportion protected

The same steps as above were followed to estimate the marine protected area and were repeated for both terrestrial and marine OECMs. Total area conserved was calculated by summing area protected and OECM area.

### Terrestrial conserved areas within each province and territory

CPCAD contains information on the province or territory in which a conserved area is located. The polygons for each terrestrial protected area within a province or territory were combined into a single polygon to calculate the area. The analysis was repeated for terrestrial OECMs.

Overlaps between provinces and territories can occur due to input from multiple stakeholders during data collection; these overlaps were accounted for in the table. In places where protected areas and OECMs overlapped, only the protected area was included in the total.

Additional analysis was then conducted to estimate the area for OECMs. In places where protected areas and OECMs overlapped, only the protected area was included in the total. ### Conserved areas, by ecological area

CPCAD does not contain information on ecological areas. To generate an estimate of conserved area within each ecozone and ecoregion, a geospatial analysis was conducted. However, national ecozone and ecoregion boundaries are more generalized than local conserved areas boundaries, and this has the potential to affect estimates in coastal areas. To avoid this problem, marine conserved area that mapped outside a marine ecozone were assigned to the nearest marine ecozone. Similarly, terrestrial conserved areas that mapped outside a terrestrial ecozone were assigned to the nearest terrestrial ecozone.

To be consistent with the projection used in CPCAD, the ecozone layer was re-projected to Albers Equal Area Conic. The total area of each ecozone was then calculated from its geospatial boundaries. The Newfoundland-Labrador Shelves ecozone area was corrected for the territorial area of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon.

The same methodology was used to calculate the conserved area within ecoregions.

### Recent changes

Since 2021, CPCAD accounts protected areas and OECMs in the year they were recognized, rather than the year they were established, as was previously the case.

### Caveats and limitations

In 2018, the Conservation Areas Reporting and Tracking System was converted to the [Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-wildlife-areas/protected-conserved-areas-database.html) (CPCAD) and brought formally within Environment and Climate Change Canada.

Data are regularly reviewed and updated. The completeness of CPCAD is continuously being improved as existing conserved areas are reviewed and added to CPCAD if appropriate. Information on the protection date for sites with previously unreported dates may influence trend calculations.

Trends are estimated based on the date a site qualified as a protected area or OECM. The totals for a previous year may change as data are updated.

Comparisons with previous reports should be made with caution, as data quality and completeness continue to improve. Privately protected land and OECMs contribute to achievement of Canada's targets, but many are not yet captured within CPCAD.

More information

The area protected or conserved calculated using polygon boundaries may differ from the "official area" reported in the [CPCAD](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-wildlife-areas/protected-conserved-areas-database.html).

Responsibility for source data accuracy and completeness lies with the data providers. Jurisdictional work in terrestrial and marine areas is guided by the federal, provincial and territorial report [One with Nature](https://publications.gc.ca/site/eng/9.857393/publication.html). In these areas, guidance material and [decision support tools](https://canadaconservation.ca/home/participate/evaluate-your-site/) were adapted from, and in collaboration with, the [Canadian Council on Ecological Areas](https://ccea-ccae.org/). Nonetheless, some differences in the approach organizations take in recognizing protected areas and OECMs can be expected.

Areas that are no longer recognized as protected or conserved ("decommissioned" or "delisted") are not captured comprehensively and may be missing from CPCAD. Decommissioned or delisted areas are counted from their establishment date until their delisting date.

Complex boundaries, such as coastlines and ecological areas, must be generalized for mapping purposes. In nature, ecozones or ecoregions do not have sharp boundaries. Due to the uncertainty of such boundaries, results should be seen as estimates rather than precise measurements. The mismatch in scale between conserved areas, mapped with fine detail, and national-scale geographic frameworks, mapped at a broad scale, may lead to minor differences across the various summaries because of the measurement uncertainty inherent in this type of analysis. Differences in the delineation of coastlines may result in a small amount of overlap between terrestrial and marine conserved area polygon boundaries; these overlaps have not been addressed.

Ecozones and ecoregions are ecologically based frameworks and should not be considered an expression of sovereignty. # Canada’s existing and proposed marine protected and conserved areas

In 2022, Canada agreed to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, a global target to protect 30% of the world's lands and oceans by 2030. Protecting the ocean within the Exclusive Economic Zone is a vital contribution if the world is to reach that collective goal.

As of May 2026

**17.65%**  
 of Canada’s marine and coastal areas are conserved

**1,015,018 km 2**  
 of Canada’s marine and coastal areas are conserved

## Types of marine protected and conserved areas

Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) include:

*   _Oceans Act MPAs_ established by Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) 
    *   MPAs established under the _Oceans Act_ can be designated either by a ministerial order regulation (with protection for up to 5 years) or by regulations made by the Governor-in-Council (for long-term designation). [Learn more about establishing MPA](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/aoi-si/index-eng.html)

*   National Marine Conservation Areas established by Parks Canada (PC)
*   Marine National Wildlife Areas and National Wildlife Areas with marine components established by Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC)
*   Provincial protected areas

Other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs), including marine refuges

*   OECM is a term used for area-based measures other than MPAs that provide long-term biodiversity outcomes. To date, all areas that qualify as OECMs have been fisheries closures. Fisheries closures that meet OECM criteria are known as marine refuges.

Please consult the [About federal marine conservation tools](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/protection-conservation/tools-outils/index-eng.html) for detailed information about the types of federal marine protected and conserved areas.

## Establishment, recognition and management processes for marine protected and conserved areas

DFO, PC and ECCC work to identify marine areas that need protection or areas where long-term conservation outcomes can be achieved through effective management measures. To do this, DFO, PC and ECCC work in collaboration with the following partners:

*   provincial and territorial governments
*   Inuit and Indigenous governments and communities
*   industry
*   stakeholders
*   environmental organizations
*   other interested Canadians

When an area needs protection, an MPA can be established under the _Oceans Act_ or the area may be recognized as a marine OECM.

A series of steps are taken to establish and manage MPAs under the _Oceans Act_, whether designated [by ministerial order (MO)](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/about-notre-sujet/publications/infographics-infographies/ministerial-order-mpa-ministeriel-vertu-zpm-eng.html) or [by Governor‑in‑Council (GiC)](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/about-notre-sujet/publications/infographics-infographies/governor-council-mpa-gouverneur-conseil-zpm-eng.html) regulations. Similarly, the process to recognize and manage OECMs involves five steps. Consultation and engagement occur at each stage of the process.

# Canada’s existing and proposed marine protected and conserved areas

In 2022, Canada agreed to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, a global target to protect 30% of the world's lands and oceans by 2030. Protecting the ocean within the Exclusive Economic Zone is a vital contribution if the world is to reach that collective goal.

As of May 2026

**17.65%**  
 of Canada’s marine and coastal areas are conserved

**1,015,018 km 2**  
 of Canada’s marine and coastal areas are conserved

## On this page

*   Types of marine protected and conserved areas
*   Establishment, recognition and management processes for marine protected and conserved areas
*   Proposed marine protected and conserved areas (DFO)
*   Existing marine protected and conserved areas (DFO)
*   Map of Canada’s existing protected and conserved areas
*   Related information

## Types of marine protected and conserved areas

Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) include:

*   _Oceans Act MPAs_ established by Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) 
    *   MPAs established under the _Oceans Act_ can be designated either by a ministerial order regulation (with protection for up to 5 years) or by regulations made by the Governor-in-Council (for long-term designation). [Learn more about establishing MPA](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/aoi-si/index-eng.html)

*   National Marine Conservation Areas established by Parks Canada (PC)
*   Marine National Wildlife Areas and National Wildlife Areas with marine components established by Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC)
*   Provincial protected areas

Other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs), including marine refuges

*   OECM is a term used for area-based measures other than MPAs that provide long-term biodiversity outcomes. To date, all areas that qualify as OECMs have been fisheries closures. Fisheries closures that meet OECM criteria are known as marine refuges.

Please consult the [About federal marine conservation tools](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/protection-conservation/tools-outils/index-eng.html) for detailed information about the types of federal marine protected and conserved areas.

## Establishment, recognition and management processes for marine protected and conserved areas

DFO, PC and ECCC work to identify marine areas that need protection or areas where long-term conservation outcomes can be achieved through effective management measures. To do this, DFO, PC and ECCC work in collaboration with the following partners:

*   provincial and territorial governments
*   Inuit and Indigenous governments and communities
*   industry
*   stakeholders
*   environmental organizations
*   other interested Canadians

When an area needs protection, an MPA can be established under the _Oceans Act_ or the area may be recognized as a marine OECM.

A series of steps are taken to establish and manage MPAs under the _Oceans Act_, whether designated [by ministerial order (MO)](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/about-notre-sujet/publications/infographics-infographies/ministerial-order-mpa-ministeriel-vertu-zpm-eng.html) or [by Governor‑in‑Council (GiC)](https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/about-notre-sujet/publications/infographics-infographies/governor-council-mpa-gouverneur-conseil-zpm-eng.html) regulations. Similarly, the process to recognize and manage OECMs involves five steps. Consultation and engagement occur at each stage of the process.

To support Canada’s commitment to protect 30% of its oceans by 2030, additional sites may be considered prior to 2030. and Conserved Areas Database (CPCAD)The Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database (CPCAD) is the authoritative source of data on protected and conserved areas in Canada. The database consists of the most up-to-date spatial and attribute data on marine and terrestrial protected areas in all governance categories recognized by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), as well as Other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs, or conserved areas) across the country. Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs) are also included if they are recognized as protected or conserved areas. CPCAD adheres to national reporting standards and is freely available to the public.

CPCAD is compiled and managed by Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC), in collaboration with federal, provincial, territorial, and other reporting authorities that provide the data. The database contains combined data from all these Canadian reporting authorities, who have determined that their areas meet the Canadian criteria as protected or conserved areas.

CPCAD is used by a wide range of organizations, including governments, environmental non-governmental organizations (ENGOs), academia, land managers, industry, and the general public. CPCAD supports many of the Government of Canada’s priorities including Canada’s national reporting on protected areas, Canada’s international reporting on protected areas as a result of Canada’s commitments under the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, and Canada’s protected areas program by providing baseline information.

More detailed information on CPCAD is available by downloading the User Manual.

The data is current as of the date of the most recent revision. The question: "two river regions with the highest proportion of sites with 'good' or 'excellent' river water quality from the 2021 to 2023 period". # Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database

This is a database of protected and other conserved areas.

## On this page

*   Introduction
*   Data and resources
*   Statistics
*   Related links

## Introduction

The Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database (CPCAD) is the national repository of the most up to date spatial and descriptive data on Canada’s terrestrial and marine protected areas (PA) and [other effective area-based conservation measures (OECM)](https://canadaconservation.ca/home/conserving-lands/oecms/). Compiled and managed by [Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change.html), CPCAD is developed in collaboration with a diverse range of partners, including federal, provincial, and territorial governments, Indigenous governments, local governments, non-governmental organizations and private landowners.

CPCAD is used by a wide range of organizations, including governments, environmental non-governmental organizations, academia, land managers, industry, and the public.

CPCAD supports:

*   Canada’s national reporting on protected and conserved areas through:
    *   Canadian Environmental Sustainability Indicators (CESI)
    *   [Federal Sustainable Development Strategy (FSDS)](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/climate-change/federal-sustainable-development-strategy.html) progress reports
    *   [Canadian Protected Areas Status Reports](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/wildlife-habitat/publications/protected-areas-report-2016-2020.html)

*   Canada’s international reporting on protected and conserved areas as a result of Canada’s commitments under the UN Convention on Biological Diversity through:
    *   Canada’s National Reports to the [UN Convention on Biological Diversity](https://www.cbd.int/)
    *   the [World Commission on Protected Areas (WCPA)](https://www.iucn.org/theme/protected-areas/our-work/world-database-protected-areas)

*   Canada’s protected areas program by providing baseline information for:
    *   the design and expansion of protected and conserved areas networks
    *   species at risk, critical habitat, and integrated conservation planning
    *   other assessments, analysis, and visualizations by diverse users

*   
Background information

### CPCAD partnerships

The CPCAD database has evolved from the Conservation Areas Reporting and Tracking System (CARTS), which was originally a collaborative initiative between ECCC and the [Canadian Council on Ecological Areas (CCEA)](https://ccea-ccae.org/). CCEA played a pivotal role in developing the foundational tools and guidance for recognizing and reporting protected areas across Canada.

Since 2018, CPCAD has been compiled and managed by ECCC in partnership with a diverse network of data providers. These include federal, provincial, and territorial governments, Indigenous organizations, local governments, environmental non-governmental organizations, and private landowners. The number of data providers continues to expand each year, strengthening a comprehensive national view of Canada’s conservation efforts.

New data providers in 2025 included:

    *   Howe Sound Biosphere Region Initiative Society
    *   Pheasant Rump Nakota First Nation

New data providers in 2024 included:

    *   Ducks Unlimited Canada
    *   Manitoba Habitat Conservancy
    *   Otipemisiwak Métis Government
    *   Transport Canada

New data providers in 2023 included:

    *   Ann and Sandy Cross Conservation Area
    *   BC Nature
    *   J.D. Irving Limited
    *   Miistakis Institute
    *   Nature Conservancy of CanadaFootnote 1
    *   Northern Biomes LTD
    *   Regional District of Central Okanagan

CPCAD is endorsed by the [Pathway initiative](https://canadaconservation.ca/home/)

# Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database

This is a database of protected and other conserved areas.

## On this page

*   Introduction
*   Data and resources
*   Statistics
*   Related links

## Introduction

The Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database (CPCAD) is the national repository of the most up to date spatial and descriptive data on Canada’s terrestrial and marine protected areas (PA) and [other effective area-based conservation measures (OECM)](https://canadaconservation.ca/home/conserving-lands/oecms/). Compiled and managed by [Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC)](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change.html), CPCAD is developed in collaboration with a diverse range of partners, including federal, provincial, and territorial governments, Indigenous governments, local governments, non-governmental organizations and private landowners.

CPCAD is used by a wide range of organizations, including governments, environmental non-governmental organizations, academia, land managers, industry, and the public.

CPCAD supports:

*   Canada’s national reporting on protected and conserved areas through:
    *   Canadian Environmental Sustainability Indicators (CESI)
    *   [Federal Sustainable Development Strategy (FSDS)](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/climate-change/federal-sustainable-development-strategy.html) progress reports
    *   [Canadian Protected Areas Status Reports](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/wildlife-habitat/publications/protected-areas-report-2016-2020.html)

*   Canada’s international reporting on protected and conserved areas as a result of Canada’s commitments under the UN Convention on Biological Diversity through:
    *   Canada’s National Reports to the [UN Convention on Biological Diversity](https://www.cbd.int/)
    *   the [World Commission on Protected Areas (WCPA)](https://www.iucn.org/theme/protected-areas/our-work/world-database-protected-areas)

*   Canada’s protected areas program by providing baseline information for:
    *   the design and expansion of protected and conserved areas networks
    *   species at risk, critical habitat, and integrated conservation planning
    *   other assessments, analysis, and visualizations by diverse users

*   
Background information

### CPCAD partnerships

The CPCAD database has evolved from the Conservation Areas Reporting and Tracking System (CARTS), which was originally a collaborative initiative between ECCC and the [Canadian Council on Ecological Areas (CCEA)](https://ccea-ccae.org/). CCEA played a pivotal role in developing the foundational tools and guidance for recognizing and reporting protected areas across Canada.

Since 2018, CPCAD has been compiled and managed by ECCC in partnership with a diverse network of data providers. These include federal, provincial, and territorial governments, Indigenous organizations, local governments, environmental non-governmental organizations, and private landowners. The number of data providers continues to expand each year, strengthening a comprehensive national view of Canada’s conservation efforts.

New data providers in 2025 included:

    *   Howe Sound Biosphere Region Initiative Society
    *   Pheasant Rump Nakota First Nation

New data providers in 2024 included:

    *   Ducks Unlimited Canada
    *   Manitoba Habitat Conservancy
    *   Otipemisiwak Métis Government
    *   Transport Canada

New data providers in 2023 included:

    *   Ann and Sandy Cross Conservation Area
    *   BC Nature
    *   J.D. Irving Limited
    *   Miistakis Institute
    *   Nature Conservancy of CanadaFootnote 1
    *   Northern Biomes LTD
    *   Regional District of Central Okanagan

CPCAD is endorsed by the [Pathway initiative](https://canadaconservation.ca/home/)

## Abstract

Canada has committed to protecting 30% of its land by 2030, yet existing protected areas cover only 12.4% of Canadian lands, which is insufficient to protect terrestrial biodiversity. In this study, we identified priority areas for biodiversity conservation in Canada, using data on 1506 species across nine taxonomic groups. We first evaluated the effectiveness of existing protected areas in conserving at-risk and other species. Then, we applied optimization algorithms to determine priority areas that could enhance the existing system. Our results reveal that over 90% of the species studied have less than 30% of their spatial distribution currently protected. To meet a constant conservation target of protecting at least 30% of the spatial distribution for all species, Canada would need to expand its protected area system by 16%–17% of its total land area, focusing on regions like Nunavut, Quebec, and the Northwest Territories. Alternatively, when using relative conservation targets based on species’ range sizes, Canada would need to prioritize expanding protected areas by 4.56%–5.46% of its land, with new areas primarily in Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec. Achieving these goals will require collaborative strategies that respect Indigenous rights and involve agreements with private landowners.

## Introduction

Protected areas (PAs) are a crucial component of strategies to alleviate the ongoing biodiversity crisis (Watson et al. 2014). Recognizing this, 196 countries including Canada agreed to the Kunming Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF) to conserve 30% of their land by 2030 (GBF 2022). More specifically, based on Target 1 of the KM-GBF, countries committed to conserving biodiversity in their spatial planning process and to bring the loss of areas with a high ecological value to zero by 2030. Target 3 of the KM-GBF urges countries to protect at least 30% of their natural habitats by 2030, using a network of well-governed conservation areas that respect Indigenous rights and ensure sustainable practices. Additionally, the KM-GBF urges implementation of actions to prevent human-induced extinctions, significantly reduce extinction risks, maintain and restore genetic diversity across species, and manage human–wildlife interactions to promote coexistence through both in situ and ex situ conservation and sustainable management practices.

Effectively implementing the KM-GBF in Canada is crucial, as the country frequently contributes to ecosystem services beyond its 7% share of global land area. This creates both an opportunity and a responsibility for Canada to lead in conservation efforts and outcomes (Coristine et al. 2019). Nevertheless, the existing PA system in Canada is inadequate for meeting the KM-GBF Targets. Despite recent progress in expanding the national PA system, PAs only cover 12.4% of the country (ECCC 2023). These areas are insufficient for protecting Canada's biodiversity and over 800 species that are identified by the federal government as at risk of extinction (SAR) (COSEWIC 2020). For example, Bolliger et al. (2020) found PAs in Canada protect an average of only 8.1% of SAR ranges. Lin et al. (2020) showed that less than 10% of priority stopover sites of migratory birds in North America are protected officially, and Hardouin and Hargreaves (2023) confirmed that current PAs only cover less than 7% of species at risk hotspots. In addition, Hardouin and Hargreaves (2023) found that a majority of nationally and globally endangered species in Canada have less than 10% of their ranges within PAs. Furthermore, Canada's PA system is least adequate in its most biodiverse areas at the southern border, which is where human populations are particularly high (Eckert et al. 2023). Thus, it is imperative that efforts to expand Canada's PA system must be designed to address current shortfalls as the country moves forward in its commitment to the KM-GBF.

Previous studies have identified priority areas for conservation in Canada among certain taxonomic groups and regions. For example, Stralberg et al. (2018) identified high priority areas for songbird species across Canada, while Lin et al. (2020) evaluated stopovers of migratory birds across North America. Proctor et al. (2022) assessed the most effective allocation of resources for habitat protection for at-risk species in Ontario, Canada. Eckert et al. (2023) undertook a prioritization analysis of land for conservation using Zonation 5 (Moilanen et al. 2022) for plants, mammals, birds, butterflies, amphibians, reptiles in Canada excluding farmlands and areas with higher human disturbance. However, such areas can play an important role in biodiversity conservation (Santos-Filho et al. 2012; Ricciardi et al. 2021; Riva and Fahrig 2022), despite higher potential barriers to conservation. More generally, traditionally underrepresented taxa such as lichens, mosses, and mollusks have not been evaluated in previous PA selection studies across Canada.

Here, we provide the most comprehensive prioritization of Canadian lands for biodiversity conservation to date. To achieve this, we used the spatial distribution layers of 48 amphibians, 48 reptiles, 161 mammals, 510 birds, 401 arthropods, 297 vascular plants, 15 lichens, 17 mosses, and 9 mollusks in Canada. After compiling spatial distribution data for each of these species, we assessed the performance of existing PAs by comparing the percentage of each species’ spatial distribution covered by protected areas to a suite of target thresholds. We then used a systematic conservation planning approach to identify priority areas for addressing target shortfalls. Since the identification of priority areas depends on the underlying objectives, we explored a range of scenarios, using a factorial design varying targets from 30% of spatial distribution to flexible targets based on spatial distribution size, and varying cost from area-equivalent costs to human footprint (Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021) as a measure of relative cost. Finally, we evaluated how expanding the existing protected area system to include the priority areas could improve conservation efforts across Canada. Our conclusions serve to help the Canadian and provincial/territorial governments and conservation practitioners working at local scales identify nationally important areas for conserving biodiversity.

## Materials and methods

### Study system

We used 1 km×1 km grid cells as planning units for the prioritization (_N_=9880 260) across Canada. Each planning unit corresponds to a distinct piece of land that may be considered for the establishment of protected areas. All species distribution data and current PA boundary data (ECCC 2023), provincial boundary (STATCAN 2016), human footprint data (Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021), and Indigenous Lands (Government of Canada 2017) were resampled and reprojected if necessary to match the spatial properties of the planning units to a 1 km 2 spatial grid.

We examined 1506 terrestrial species across nine taxonomic groups in Canada. To achieve this, we compiled data from several sources (Table S1). From these species’ distribution datasets, we included data that delimited the presence and absence of species in particular locations (e.g., range polygons) and, where available, continuous data that delineated the abundance or habitat suitability of species in particular locations (e.g., species distribution models). We applied thresholds to the continuous datasets to standardize data across taxa (see Table S1 for details).

Although the complete dataset of 1506 species represent only a small portion of the over 47 000 native species in Canada (CESCC 2022), it encompasses a reasonably representative sample of Canada's terrestrial biodiversity given the breadth of taxa included. When distribution data for SAR species (COSEWIC 2020) were available from other sources, such as the Area of Habitat (AOH) map (Proctor et al. 2022; Schuster et al. 2023), we prioritized these over range data (Bolliger et al. 2020). The AOH maps align species ranges with terrestrial land cover datasets and elevation data to more accurately define the species’ AOH (Brook et al. 2019; Schuster et al. 2023). For migratory bird species present in the eBird dataset, we accommodated their migratory habitat requirements by treating their migratory and resident distributions as separate features in the prioritization (Butchart et al. 2015). We accessed the eBird database ([www.ebird.org](http://www.ebird.org/)) through the ebirdst R package v2.2021.1 (Auer et al. 2020; Auer et al. 2023). All analyses were performed in the R statistical computing environment v4.3.2 (R Core Team 2023).

### Representation targets

Representation targets specify the minimum percentage of a species’ (or ecosystems’) distribution that should ideally be protected to safeguard their long-term persistence (Friedrichs et al. 2018; González-Fernández et al. 2022). Since it can be difficult to set targets that are both meaningful for informing policy and for reducing extinction risk (MacKinnon et al. 2015), we examined two approaches for setting targets. Specifically, the approaches involve setting targets as (i) a constant 30% of species range, informed by the more general goals of protecting an ecologically representative 30% of land area (GBF 2022); and (ii) a variable percentage of each species’ total distribution, setting higher percentages for species with smaller distributions (Rodrigues et al. 2004; Hanson et al. 2020). In the second approach, for the species with a spatial extent smaller than 1000 km 2, we considered a 100% target (8 amphibians, 26 arthropods, 307 birds, 7 mammals, 3 reptiles, 21 vascular plants). For the species with a spatial extent larger than 1000 000 km 2 we considered a target of 100 000 km 2 (17 amphibians, 181 arthropods, 753 birds, 80 mammals, 5 reptiles, 12 vascular plants), and for the species with an intermediate spatial extent (between 1000 and 250 000 km 2), we assigned targets by loglinearly interpolating between these spatial extent thresholds with 10% and 100% target thresholds and used the 10% target for the species with a range of up to 1000 000 km 2.

### Protected area assessment

To assess the performance of existing protected areas, we overlaid species’ distributions with protected areas and calculated the percentage of each species’ distribution that was covered by existing PAs. We then compared each species’ representation by existing PAs to its targets (computed using the two approaches described above). Additionally, we identified species that are entirely absent from the existing protected areas.

### Spatial prioritizations

We generated spatial prioritizations under four different scenarios (Table 1). These scenarios represent a factorial design to examine the influence of different effective target settings and costs associated with establishing protected areas. Specifically, the analysis involved identifying priority areas using (i) loglinear targets and equal planning unit costs, (ii) loglinear targets and the human footprint index(Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021) for planning unit costs, (iii) constant (30%) targets and equal planning unit costs, and (iv) constant (30%) targets and the human footprint index for planning unit costs. We used the human footprint index as a cost metric in some scenarios because it is a useful index to reflect the potential complexity of planning in landscapes that are heavily used by humans (Venter et al. 2016; Tapia-Armijos et al. 2017; Schuster et al. 2019 _a_; Hardouin and Hargreaves 2023). However, we acknowledge that it is not a complete representation of human impacts on landscapes (Nolte 2020; Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021). Across all scenarios, we generated prioritizations using the minimum set formulation of the PA selection problem (see Beyer et al. 2016 for mathematical formulation). Briefly, this formulation identifies the cheapest set of planning units needed to meet the species’ representation targets. To account for existing conservation efforts, we locked in planning units covered by existing protected areas (see Fig. S2 for additional counterfactual scenarios that did not lock in existing PAs). As research has suggested that Indigenous stewardship of their lands supports high biodiversity levels that are comparable to protected regions (Schuster et al. 2019 _b_), we reran separate scenarios in which we also locked in Indigenous lands in addition to current protected areas. This is meant to reflect effective Indigenous stewardship of biodiversity. However, this does not imply that national governments have the authority to count these lands toward their conservation targets. All prioritizations were generated to optimality using the prioritizr R package (Hanson et al. 2023) and Gurobi optimization software (Gurobi Optimization 2023).

## Results

### Performance of existing protected areas

On average, the percentage of spatial distribution located within current PAs is higher for terrestrial SAR species than non-SAR species, across all groups except reptiles (Fig. 1). Currently, Canada's PAs fail to reach our 30% coverage goal for 1405 species (93% of species in our dataset). This includes 375 SAR (87.6% of SAR in our analysis). For 1295 species (86% of species in our dataset), including 344 SAR, less than 20% of spatial distribution are protected and for 791 species (52.5%), including 229 SAR, less than 10% of spatial distribution are protected. Based on a constant 30% target, mosses and arthropods are the groups with the highest and lowest percentages of species protected in Canada (18% and 3%, respectively). However, based on loglinear targets, mammals are the group with the highest percentage of species protected (49%) and both mollusks and mosses have no species adequately protected (Fig. 1).

When multiple conservation features were available for one species, we considered the species as not-protected when spatial distribution of one or more features within protected areas were less than defined targets.

### Prioritization scenarios

Our prioritization scenarios suggest that between 455 191 and 1714 470 km 2 (4.56%–17.17% of Canada's lands) of new PA would be needed to meet our species-based targets, with the lower value being for the scenario where all planning units have the same costs and the target was loglinear, and the upper value being for the scenario where human footprint was used as a cost layer and 30% of the spatial distribution of all species were required to be selected (Fig. 2). These numbers changed to 384 987–1198 719 km 2 when we locked in Indigenous lands in addition to current protected areas (Fig. S3). The land requirements for the counterfactual scenario where protected areas could be swapped suggest that between 904 717 and 2824 082 km 2 lands were needed to protect the conservation features (Fig. S2), implying that some current areas in the PA network may have redundancy in the species that they protect.

In scenarios with 30% as a constant target for all species, Nunavut, Quebec, and Northwest Territories had the largest land areas selected including current and new PAs, even after locking in Indigenous lands. This result is due to the preponderance of wide-ranged species at higher latitude in Canada, including such as woodland caribou (_Rangifer tarandus_), wolverine (_Gulo gulo_), ermine (_Mustela erminea_), Old World swallowtail (_Papilio Machaon_), common redpoll (_Acanthis flammea_), and polar bumble bee (_Bombus polaris_). In scenarios with loglinear targets, British Columbia, Nunavut, and Quebec are the provinces with the highest selected lands as PAs regardless of including Indigenous lands in the solution or not. When Indigenous lands were not included, Nunavut and Quebec and Northwest Territories have the largest percentage of recommended new PA for a constant 30% target, while Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec are the provinces with the largest percentage of recommended new PA for loglinear targets. However, when Indigenous lands are included, Quebec, Ontario, and Alberta have the highest percentage of new protected areas for a constant 30% target, and British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec are the provinces with the highest percentages for the loglinear targets (Tables 2 and S3).

## Discussion

We used both species-based and a constant 30% targets to prioritize potential land area for conservation, based on Canada's commitment to protect a representative 30% of its terrestrial area. We assumed that by protecting 30% of the spatial distribution of its species, Canada would likely be achieving such representation. A gap analysis indicates that for around 93% of 1506 species investigated, less than 30% of their spatial distributions in Canada are adequately represented by protected areas. Furthermore, for around half of these species, less than 10% of their spatial distributions are within the current PAs. We also used a flexible targeting approach based on species’ range sizes. Our systematic conservation planning results indicated that, based on various metrics included in scenarios, an additional 4.56%–17.17% of Canada is needed to be protected to meet either flexible spatial distribution-based targets or 30% spatial distribution targets in Canada.

Our analysis revealed that while mammals, like many other taxa, are significantly underrepresented in current PAs, their representation is higher compared to other taxa. This result is consistent with previous studies that have globally confirmed the taxonomic bias toward mammals and birds in conservation (e.g., Titley et al. 2017). However, our study did not find a bias towards birds, possibly because we considered migratory birds as underrepresented if either their breeding or migratory habitats within Canada did not meet the defined conservation targets. Conversely, the current PA system appears to be least effective in protecting terrestrial reptiles, mollusks, vascular plants, and lichens. Fewer than 20% of species in these groups are adequately represented in current PAs. This is not surprising, as these taxa are often overlooked in conservation research (Donaldson et al. 2017) or management (Evans et al. 2016; Creighton and Bennett 2019; Mammola et al. 2020)

Although we expected a high percentage of priority areas to be located within British Columbia, Quebec, and Ontario, the provinces that host the highest number of species (Fig. S1), our results suggest that there can be some exceptions in this regard. Nunavut, which hosts fewer species than many other Canadian jurisdictions, was one of the two provinces with the highest percentage of newly added PAs when we used a constant 30% target and regardless of the cost type assigned to the planning units and even without locking in the current PAs (Table S2). This result likely emerges because there are some unique species or migratory cycle habitats that depend on these areas, such as long-tailed duck (_Clangula hyemalis_), buff-bellied pipit (_Anthus rubescens_), northern collared lemming (_Dicrostonyx groenlandicus_), and Old World swallowtail (_Papilio machaon_).

Considering relative targets for different species could result in PA system that are potentially more biologically meaningful and more feasible than fixed targets. When we assign a uniform representation target of 30% to all species, we may consider species with very limited spatial distribution to be well-represented, even if PA covers only 30% of their limited range. Conversely, the 30% target represents a vast land area for widespread Canadian species that can inhabit large swaths of northern regions.

Counterfactual scenarios suggest some redundancy in Canada's PA system (Fig. S2). For example, when we set conservation targets using a loglinear function, 16.35%–27.19% less total PA required compared to current conditions. However, we note that there are many reasons for establishing PAs beyond protecting species’ ranges or habitats (Neugarten et al. 2024), and we also note that managing current PAs may be much more efficient in general than establishing and then managing new ones (Adams et al. 2019). Thus, given Canada's general shortfall in PA coverage, we do not recommend removing areas from the current PA portfolio.

When Indigenous lands were locked-in in addition to the current protected areas, an additional 3.9%–12.0% of Canada are theoretically needed to be protected to meet either flexible or constant 30% spatial distribution targets in Canada. We note that it is inappropriate to include Indigenous sovereign lands as “protected” in Canada's national protected areas system. However, our result does suggest that mutually agreed partnerships could be an important way forward to improve biodiversity protection in Canada. An example of a program that helps to facilitate this is the Project Finance for Permanence Program, which facilitates public and private funding for establishing and sustaining Indigenous protected areas (Government of Canada 2024).

Our results also indicate that protecting some areas with high human footprint may be very important for an effective biodiversity conservation, as the proportion of increased protected areas in these regions was 1.8–10.3 times higher in comparison to the rest of the study area (Table S4). This result is not surprising because many species, including SAR species, can be present in the human-dominated regions (Allan et al. 2019; OMECP 2019). This is especially the case in Canada, where high biodiversity areas in the south often coincide with high human populations and land pressure (Coristine et al. 2019; Proctor et al. 2022).

Our results differ from the most recent national-scale prioritization by Eckert et al. (2023) in two main aspects. First, Eckert et al. (2023) found that in national scenarios, 65% of their studied species will meet the 30% protection goal, which is equivalent to around 2598 380 km 2. Our results however indicated that if we increase the PA system to 2.1–2.4 times its current size (equivalent to maximum 2957 024 km 2 in total), all the species considered in our analysis will have at least 30% of their spatial distribution protected. One possible reason for this discrepancy can be different species used in our study versus what was used in Eckert et al. (2023). In their study, the taxa with the highest number of features in prioritization were plants; however, in our study birds had the highest number of conservation features. Second, in two scenarios we assigned a higher cost to the planning units (pixels) with higher human disturbance/footprint, while in Eckert et al. (2023), agricultural and highly disturbed areas were excluded from the analysis. Another explanation could be the optimization algorithms used in two studies. While Eckert et al. (2023) used Zonation 5 (Moilanen et al. 2022), which uses an iterative algorithm based on marginal loss for identifying near-optimal solutions, we used integer programming techniques that guarantee optimality.

Economic cost and feasibility are increasingly recognized as crucial considerations in conservation (Joseph et al. 2009; Wilson et al. 2009). Such consideration can lead to more realistic solutions. For example, Schuster et al. (2019 _a_) found that although considering human disturbance in conservation planning may require increased total PA, for some species, like migratory species, it is an important consideration as these species depend on a combination of intact and disturbed areas. Similar to Schuster et al. (2019 _a_), our analysis found that to protect 30% of species range, scenarios with human disturbance as cost require 4.2%–5.3% greater area than scenarios assigning a similar cost value to all the planning units (Fig. 2).

Our datasets represent a large number of Canadian species (including all listed terrestrial SAR that have been mapped), but they do not represent all taxa and facets of biodiversity in Canada. There are therefore possibilities for future improvements. For example, Indigenous knowledge was not included in our species spatial distribution estimates, nor was detailed habitat information beyond land cover types in species distribution models. In some cases, like vascular plants, arthropods, and birds, the resolution of the raster layers was coarser than our planning unit's size, and were resampled to the same resolution as the planning units (Table S1). In addition, we only considered species ranges and AOH in the prioritization process; however, contributing population-related variables for all the species in the prioritization can result in more robust results.

It is also important to note that our prioritization does not reflect all of the values and rights that are important in the process of area-based biodiversity prioritization, especially at the finer scales where actual land-use decisions will be made. In particular, we have not included Indigenous rights and values. For actual protection decisions, a more comprehensive approach that is led or co-led by Indigenous partners would be necessary, given that Canada is composed of traditional Indigenous territories. We also note that in many cases, Indigenous-led protection may take quite different forms to the target-based protection that is the focus of Canada's government. In addition, in areas where remnant habitats are confined to small but vital areas (Riva and Fahrig 2022), it will be important to carefully evaluate cost tradeoffs (Proctor et al. 2022) and consider alternative options such as private land stewardship programs. Furthermore, it is worth noting that our prioritization does not advise on the management actions that may need to be implemented inside priority areas to effectively conserve biodiversity (e.g., habitat restoration, invasive species management) (Tallis et al. 2021; Salgado-Rojas et al. 2023). A more comprehensive approach may also need to address various additional ecological, biological, and human-related factors (Haines et al. 2012).

## Conclusions

Our results show that we need to add between 1594 843 and 1714 470 km 2 to our current PA system to protect 30% of the spatial distribution of 1506 species in Canada (including terrestrial species at risk and native species such as migratory and resident birds, mammals, reptile, amphibians, bumblebees and butterflies, vascular plants, lichens, mosses, and mollusks), This means that Canada needs to more than double our current PAs of 1242 554 km 2. Considering both biodiversity and feasibility, the largest area additions would be in Ontario, British Columbia, Quebec if relative targets for the study species were used, and Nunavut, Quebec, and Northwest Territories if a constant 30% target for all the study species were used (Fig. 2; Table 2).

Given the vast area requirements for meeting Canada's biodiversity commitments, the task of conserving Canada's biodiversity will likely require challenging decisions for which areas to protect. It will likely also require creative approaches for places where protection is logistically or politically impossible. Partnerships with Indigenous rights holders will be crucial to achieving the letter and spirit of Canada's biodiversity protection commitment (ECCC 2024). Agreements with private landowners, and even temporary protection areas (Wen et al. 2023), may also play important supporting roles. For example, northern Canada contains large, intact landscapes with generally fewer competing land uses than in the south but requires support for Indigenous leadership and collaboration. Expansion in southern Canada will also require support for Indigenous leadership and collaboration but may face more numerous land use conflicts. Agreements with private landowners and even temporary arrangements (where permanence is unfeasible) will thus be important for conservation in southern Canada's biodiversity hotspots.

The output of our study provides a large-scale baseline for these finer-scale next steps by identifying the areas with the highest priority for the conservation of both at-risk and native species.

## Abstract

Canada has committed to protecting 30% of its land by 2030, yet existing protected areas cover only 12.4% of Canadian lands, which is insufficient to protect terrestrial biodiversity. In this study, we identified priority areas for biodiversity conservation in Canada, using data on 1506 species across nine taxonomic groups. We first evaluated the effectiveness of existing protected areas in conserving at-risk and other species. Then, we applied optimization algorithms to determine priority areas that could enhance the existing system. Our results reveal that over 90% of the species studied have less than 30% of their spatial distribution currently protected. To meet a constant conservation target of protecting at least 30% of the spatial distribution for all species, Canada would need to expand its protected area system by 16%–17% of its total land area, focusing on regions like Nunavut, Quebec, and the Northwest Territories. Alternatively, when using relative conservation targets based on species’ range sizes, Canada would need to prioritize expanding protected areas by 4.56%–5.46% of its land, with new areas primarily in Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec. Achieving these goals will require collaborative strategies that respect Indigenous rights and involve agreements with private landowners.

## Introduction

Protected areas (PAs) are a crucial component of strategies to alleviate the ongoing biodiversity crisis (Watson et al. 2014). Recognizing this, 196 countries including Canada agreed to the Kunming Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF) to conserve 30% of their land by 2030 (GBF 2022). More specifically, based on Target 1 of the KM-GBF, countries committed to conserving biodiversity in their spatial planning process and to bring the loss of areas with a high ecological value to zero by 2030. Target 3 of the KM-GBF urges countries to protect at least 30% of their natural habitats by 2030, using a network of well-governed conservation areas that respect Indigenous rights and ensure sustainable practices. Additionally, the KM-GBF urges implementation of actions to prevent human-induced extinctions, significantly reduce extinction risks, maintain and restore genetic diversity across species, and manage human–wildlife interactions to promote coexistence through both in situ and ex situ conservation and sustainable management practices.

Effectively implementing the KM-GBF in Canada is crucial, as the country frequently contributes to ecosystem services beyond its 7% share of global land area. This creates both an opportunity and a responsibility for Canada to lead in conservation efforts and outcomes (Coristine et al. 2019). Nevertheless, the existing PA system in Canada is inadequate for meeting the KM-GBF Targets. Despite recent progress in expanding the national PA system, PAs only cover 12.4% of the country (ECCC 2023). These areas are insufficient for protecting Canada's biodiversity and over 800 species that are identified by the federal government as at risk of extinction (SAR) (COSEWIC 2020). For example, Bolliger et al. (2020) found PAs in Canada protect an average of only 8.1% of SAR ranges. Lin et al. (2020) showed that less than 10% of priority stopover sites of migratory birds in North America are protected officially, and Hardouin and Hargreaves (2023) confirmed that current PAs only cover less than 7% of species at risk hotspots. In addition, Hardouin and Hargreaves (2023) found that a majority of nationally and globally endangered species in Canada have less than 10% of their ranges within PAs. Furthermore, Canada's PA system is least adequate in its most biodiverse areas at the southern border, which is where human populations are particularly high (Eckert et al. 2023). Thus, it is imperative that efforts to expand Canada's PA system must be designed to address current shortfalls as the country moves forward in its commitment to the KM-GBF.

Previous studies have identified priority areas for conservation in Canada among certain taxonomic groups and regions. For example, Stralberg et al. (2018) identified high priority areas for songbird species across Canada, while Lin et al. (2020) evaluated stopovers of migratory birds across North America. Proctor et al. (2022) assessed the most effective allocation of resources for habitat protection for at-risk species in Ontario, Canada. Eckert et al. (2023) undertook a prioritization analysis of land for conservation using Zonation 5 (Moilanen et al. 2022) for plants, mammals, birds, butterflies, amphibians, reptiles in Canada excluding farmlands and areas with higher human disturbance. However, such areas can play an important role in biodiversity conservation (Santos-Filho et al. 2012; Ricciardi et al. 2021; Riva and Fahrig 2022), despite higher potential barriers to conservation. More generally, traditionally underrepresented taxa such as lichens, mosses, and mollusks have not been evaluated in previous PA selection studies across Canada.

Here, we provide the most comprehensive prioritization of Canadian lands for biodiversity conservation to date. To achieve this, we used the spatial distribution layers of 48 amphibians, 48 reptiles, 161 mammals, 510 birds, 401 arthropods, 297 vascular plants, 15 lichens, 17 mosses, and 9 mollusks in Canada. After compiling spatial distribution data for each of these species, we assessed the performance of existing PAs by comparing the percentage of each species’ spatial distribution covered by protected areas to a suite of target thresholds. We then used a systematic conservation planning approach to identify priority areas for addressing target shortfalls. Since the identification of priority areas depends on the underlying objectives, we explored a range of scenarios, using a factorial design varying targets from 30% of spatial distribution to flexible targets based on spatial distribution size, and varying cost from area-equivalent costs to human footprint (Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021) as a measure of relative cost. Finally, we evaluated how expanding the existing protected area system to include the priority areas could improve conservation efforts across Canada. Our conclusions serve to help the Canadian and provincial/territorial governments and conservation practitioners working at local scales identify nationally important areas for conserving biodiversity.

## Materials and methods

### Study system

We used 1 km×1 km grid cells as planning units for the prioritization (_N_=9880 260) across Canada. Each planning unit corresponds to a distinct piece of land that may be considered for the establishment of protected areas. All species distribution data and current PA boundary data (ECCC 2023), provincial boundary (STATCAN 2016), human footprint data (Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021), and Indigenous Lands (Government of Canada 2017) were resampled and reprojected if necessary to match the spatial properties of the planning units to a 1 km 2 spatial grid.

We examined 1506 terrestrial species across nine taxonomic groups in Canada. To achieve this, we compiled data from several sources (Table S1). From these species’ distribution datasets, we included data that delimited the presence and absence of species in particular locations (e.g., range polygons) and, where available, continuous data that delineated the abundance or habitat suitability of species in particular locations (e.g., species distribution models). We applied thresholds to the continuous datasets to standardize data across taxa (see Table S1 for details).

Although the complete dataset of 1506 species represent only a small portion of the over 47 000 native species in Canada (CESCC 2022), it encompasses a reasonably representative sample of Canada's terrestrial biodiversity given the breadth of taxa included. When distribution data for SAR species (COSEWIC 2020) were available from other sources, such as the Area of Habitat (AOH) map (Proctor et al. 2022; Schuster et al. 2023), we prioritized these over range data (Bolliger et al. 2020). The AOH maps align species ranges with terrestrial land cover datasets and elevation data to more accurately define the species’ AOH (Brook et al. 2019; Schuster et al. 2023). For migratory bird species present in the eBird dataset, we accommodated their migratory habitat requirements by treating their migratory and resident distributions as separate features in the prioritization (Butchart et al. 2015). We accessed the eBird database ([www.ebird.org](http://www.ebird.org/)) through the ebirdst R package v2.2021.1 (Auer et al. 2020; Auer et al. 2023). All analyses were performed in the R statistical computing environment v4.3.2 (R Core Team 2023).

### Representation targets

Representation targets specify the minimum percentage of a species’ (or ecosystems’) distribution that should ideally be protected to safeguard their long-term persistence (Friedrichs et al. 2018; González-Fernández et al. 2022). Since it can be difficult to set targets that are both meaningful for informing policy and for reducing extinction risk (MacKinnon et al. 2015), we examined two approaches for setting targets. Specifically, the approaches involve setting targets as (i) a constant 30% of species range, informed by the more general goals of protecting an ecologically representative 30% of land area (GBF 2022); and (ii) a variable percentage of each species’ total distribution, setting higher percentages for species with smaller distributions (Rodrigues et al. 2004; Hanson et al. 2020). In the second approach, for the species with a spatial extent smaller than 1000 km 2, we considered a 100% target (8 amphibians, 26 arthropods, 307 birds, 7 mammals, 3 reptiles, 21 vascular plants). For the species with a spatial extent larger than 1000 000 km 2 we considered a target of 100 000 km 2 (17 amphibians, 181 arthropods, 753 birds, 80 mammals, 5 reptiles, 12 vascular plants), and for the species with an intermediate spatial extent (between 1000 and 250 000 km 2), we assigned targets by loglinearly interpolating between these spatial extent thresholds with 10% and 100% target thresholds and used the 10% target for the species with a range of up to 1000 000 km 2.

### Protected area assessment

To assess the performance of existing protected areas, we overlaid species’ distributions with protected areas and calculated the percentage of each species’ distribution that was covered by existing PAs. We then compared each species’ representation by existing PAs to its targets (computed using the two approaches described above). Additionally, we identified species that are entirely absent from the existing protected areas.

### Spatial prioritizations

We generated spatial prioritizations under four different scenarios (Table 1). These scenarios represent a factorial design to examine the influence of different effective target settings and costs associated with establishing protected areas. Specifically, the analysis involved identifying priority areas using (i) loglinear targets and equal planning unit costs, (ii) loglinear targets and the human footprint index(Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021) for planning unit costs, (iii) constant (30%) targets and equal planning unit costs, and (iv) constant (30%) targets and the human footprint index for planning unit costs. We used the human footprint index as a cost metric in some scenarios because it is a useful index to reflect the potential complexity of planning in landscapes that are heavily used by humans (Venter et al. 2016; Tapia-Armijos et al. 2017; Schuster et al. 2019 _a_; Hardouin and Hargreaves 2023). However, we acknowledge that it is not a complete representation of human impacts on landscapes (Nolte 2020; Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2021). Across all scenarios, we generated prioritizations using the minimum set formulation of the PA selection problem (see Beyer et al. 2016 for mathematical formulation). Briefly, this formulation identifies the cheapest set of planning units needed to meet the species’ representation targets. To account for existing conservation efforts, we locked in planning units covered by existing protected areas (see Fig. S2 for additional counterfactual scenarios that did not lock in existing PAs). As research has suggested that Indigenous stewardship of their lands supports high biodiversity levels that are comparable to protected regions (Schuster et al. 2019 _b_), we reran separate scenarios in which we also locked in Indigenous lands in addition to current protected areas. This is meant to reflect effective Indigenous stewardship of biodiversity. However, this does not imply that national governments have the authority to count these lands toward their conservation targets. All prioritizations were generated to optimality using the prioritizr R package (Hanson et al. 2023) and Gurobi optimization software (Gurobi Optimization 2023).

## Results

### Performance of existing protected areas

On average, the percentage of spatial distribution located within current PAs is higher for terrestrial SAR species than non-SAR species, across all groups except reptiles (Fig. 1). Currently, Canada's PAs fail to reach our 30% coverage goal for 1405 species (93% of species in our dataset). This includes 375 SAR (87.6% of SAR in our analysis). For 1295 species (86% of species in our dataset), including 344 SAR, less than 20% of spatial distribution are protected and for 791 species (52.5%), including 229 SAR, less than 10% of spatial distribution are protected. Based on a constant 30% target, mosses and arthropods are the groups with the highest and lowest percentages of species protected in Canada (18% and 3%, respectively). However, based on loglinear targets, mammals are the group with the highest percentage of species protected (49%) and both mollusks and mosses have no species adequately protected (Fig. 1).

### Prioritization scenarios

Our prioritization scenarios suggest that between 455 191 and 1714 470 km 2 (4.56%–17.17% of Canada's lands) of new PA would be needed to meet our species-based targets, with the lower value being for the scenario where all planning units have the same costs and the target was loglinear, and the upper value being for the scenario where human footprint was used as a cost layer and 30% of the spatial distribution of all species were required to be selected (Fig. 2). These numbers changed to 384 987–1198 719 km 2 when we locked in Indigenous lands in addition to current protected areas (Fig. S3). The land requirements for the counterfactual scenario where protected areas could be swapped suggest that between 904 717 and 2824 082 km 2 lands were needed to protect the conservation features (Fig. S2), implying that some current areas in the PA network may have redundancy in the species that they protect.

In scenarios with 30% as a constant target for all species, Nunavut, Quebec, and Northwest Territories had the largest land areas selected including current and new PAs, even after locking in Indigenous lands. This result is due to the preponderance of wide-ranged species at higher latitude in Canada, including such as woodland caribou (_Rangifer tarandus_), wolverine (_Gulo gulo_), ermine (_Mustela erminea_), Old World swallowtail (_Papilio Machaon_), common redpoll (_Acanthis flammea_), and polar bumble bee (_Bombus polaris_). In scenarios with loglinear targets, British Columbia, Nunavut, and Quebec are the provinces with the highest selected lands as PAs regardless of including Indigenous lands in the solution or not. When Indigenous lands were not included, Nunavut and Quebec and Northwest Territories have the largest percentage of recommended new PA for a constant 30% target, while Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec are the provinces with the largest percentage of recommended new PA for loglinear targets. However, when Indigenous lands are included, Quebec, Ontario, and Alberta have the highest percentage of new protected areas for a constant 30% target, and British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec are the provinces with the highest percentages for the loglinear targets (Tables 2 and S3).
