## 3. River water quality process studies

Process-based or mechanistic studies rely on experimental research and mathematical relationships to computationally characterize and explain multi-parameter processes in aquatic systems. Given that confounding issues (i.e., climate change, pollution, changing hydrology) collectively contribute to changing water quality, both advanced monitoring and experimental tools that seek to understand observations mechanistically, are required to inform more complex modeling activities. When more physical, chemical, and biological riverine factors are considered or understood, resultant models are more holistic with strengthened predictive capacity.

Rivers and streams present a unique challenge for process-based studies due to their dynamic complexity, not only in terms of hydrological processes, but also cooperatively intertwined biological and chemical processes. As such, while the determination of water quantity is inextricably linked to modeling of water quality, river flow processes (e.g., hydrology, hydrometry, bathymetry) are not explicitly discussed in this review because there are ongoing extensive efforts to model water quantity at a national scale, as previously described. In Canada, where cold-climate watersheds experience the complex dynamics of river ice during the winter months, and the subsequent spring break-up, ice processes must be integrated into these multi-disciplinary studies to understand the implications on aquatic ecosystems. The layers of complexity further multiply as point and nonpoint source pollutants enter these dynamics systems, influencing water quality downstream. Further, ongoing and emerging research in both academic and government sectors across Canada seek to address some outstanding knowledge gaps as they pertain to understanding and modeling various water quality variables.

### 3.1. Physical processes

#### 3.1.1. River water temperature

Water temperature exerts a critical control on aquatic ecosystem dynamics and influences bio-geochemical processes (Caissie 2006; Hannah and Garner 2015; Ramulifho et al. 2018). River water temperature is a result of dynamic, scale-dependent, and spatially and temporally variable processes such as climate, hydrology, physiography, geomorphology, and land use (Daigle et al. 2022). It is also a key driver of heat and freshwater fluxes to oceans that affect stratification, circulation, sea ice cover, and heat budget (Yang et al. 2014, 2021; Nummelin et al. 2016; Park et al. 2020). Understanding water temperature facilitates understanding of the complex interaction of different drivers affecting thermal dynamics, such as ice on and open water periods, the cumulative impacts of human activities, and the cascading effect of changing temperature on ecological processes (Ouellet et al. 2020).

A major issue with the historical river temperature observations in Canada is the sparsity of data, which is usually based on a few spot measurements in a year (Moore 2013; Rosencranz et al. 2021). Specifically, Shrestha et al. (2024) compiled observed river temperature records from various Federal and Provincial archives across Canada and found only 106 stations that have 50 water temperature observations of>0° C over the years 1980–2018. The sparsity is especially acute for northern rivers, as only 20 of 106 stations are in Nunavut, Northwest Territories, and Yukon. Canada lacks a national database of observed water temperature. Instead, databases are regionally specific (e.g., RivTemp in eastern Canada; Boyer et al. 2016). Readers are referred to Shrestha et al. (2024) for a list of available river temperature data resources. Additionally, water temperature records from urban water treatment plants, mines, and industries (where available) could be useful to assess the effects of point sources on river water temperature. Furthermore, model-based reconstruction can supplement sparse historical observations, as demonstrated by the recent study that reconstructed water temperature records by using air2stream model for 55 stations across western Canada (Shrestha and Pesklevits 2023 _b_). The reconstructed dataset has been extended to 106 stations across Canada and is available through the Government of Canada data portal (GoC 2023 _c_).

#### 3.1.2. Ice formation, growth, and breakup

Ice formation dynamics in rivers modifies the physical characteristics of the flow in different ways, depending on stream size and slope (Ashton 1986; Prowse and Gridley 1993; Prowse 2001; Beltaos 2008, 2013 _a_). The simplest configuration of an ice-forming river occurs during the winter season in relatively large streams, and typically involves a continuous, floating ice cover of relatively uniform thickness and bottom roughness. As in open-water river flow, various particulate or dissolved substances that enter the flow domain of an ice laden river, either by natural or by anthropogenic processes, are continuously advected and spread out by the flow, while being subject to decay, enhancement, and deposition processes (Beltaos and Arora 1988; Putz and Smith 1998; Putz et al. 2000; Sabokruhie et al. 2021). Molecular and turbulent diffusion, transverse and longitudinal dispersion also operate in ice forming rivers, in which the bottom of a floating ice cover is a second boundary where the flow velocity must vanish, as it does at the riverbed.

Water quality prediction during the transitional periods of freezeup and breakup is complicated by occasional formation of ice jams comprising porous accumulations of frazil ice and (or) ice blocks, with typical aggregate thickness of a few to several meters. The porous and very rough nature of the bottom of such accumulations is a very different flow boundary from that of a solid sheet-ice cover; and this likely affects various water-quality parameters in ways that so far remain difficult to model. By modifying the spatial variation of the bed shear stress, ice jams can also cause localized riverbed erosion and deposition, which has been experimentally documented (Wuebben 1988; Hirshfield and Sui 2011) and can be built into river ice models. A special type of freezeup ice jam is the so-called “hanging dam”, which primarily forms by transport and deposition of slush under a previously formed sheet ice cover over a quiescent river reach. Hanging dams can attain thicknesses amounting to tens of meters and they are much less permeable than ordinary ice jams. In addition to causing occasional flooding, hanging dams impact aquatic life (Cunjak et al. 1998; Brown et al. 2000).

A unique type of river wave is generated upon abrupt release of an ice jam, typically during the breakup of the winter ice cover. It is termed “jave” (jam-release wave) and often attended by highly dynamic effects, such as rapidly rising water levels and extreme hydrodynamic forces applied on channel boundaries (Beltaos 2013 _b_). Field observations and measurements indicate that bank/bed erosion, as well as large pulses of suspended sediment concentration can result from major javes (Beltaos and Burrell 2021), which are often capable of dislodging and mobilizing the stationary ice cover downstream of the “parent” jam, as they propagate under it. Although the hydrodynamic characteristics of javes can be modeled (She and Hicks 2006; Shen 2010; Ye and She 2021), their impacts on water quality and aquatic life cannot be quantitatively predicted at present.

Ice processes in relatively small, shallow, steep, or mountain rivers may be very different from those just described. The ice cover of such streams may be intermittent and often grounded rather than floating. Anchor ice, which also forms in larger streams, is a prominent fall and winter feature of small rivers. It can have a variety of impacts on water quality and stream ecology associated with the substrate. Anchor ice may attain sufficient height to create an ice dam, raising upstream water levels, and potentially causing overbank inundation. When anchor ice releases from the riverbed, it can “pluck” and transport significant amounts of sediment, and even large boulders (Kalke et al. 2017; Nafziger et al. 2017; Kempema et al. 2020). Although physical processes associated with anchor ice are included in some river ice models, there is no modeling capability for water quality impacts in small streams, for which the state of science remains in the observational stage.

#### 3.1.3. Sediment dynamics

Sediment transport and dynamics are other processes with significant but poorly understood implications for water quality. The loading and transport of sediments into rivers and streams is not only troublesome in terms of turbidity impairing water quality, but also due to the concomitant processes such as nutrient loading (through absorption/desorption), contaminant transport, biofilm/floc dynamics, etc. that pose significant threats to water quality. The delivery of sediments has been studied in several key areas, notably the Peace, Athabasca, and Slave rivers that form the headwaters of the Mackenzie River basin. Here, research has assessed the transport of sediments and associated contaminants downstream into depositional zones to better understand the influences on water quality, biological health, and overall ecosystem health. Additionally, the Athabasca River presents an interesting case study by which to study the impacts of natural and anthropogenically influenced riverine systems, where research has assessed the transport of particulates and associated bituminous compounds (Droppo et al. 2018, 2019) alongside biological markers (Yergeau et al. 2013; Reid et al. 2020) indicative of hydrocarbon exposures through to the depositional environment of the Lower Athabasca River (LAR). In the Athabasca Oil Sands Region and the further downstream reaches that feed the Peace-Athabasca Delta, into and along the Mackenzie River, further research has sought to understand the fate and transport of sediment and sediment-associated PAHs in an ecological context (Evans et al. 2016; Culp et al. 2021). In the lower Mackenzie River Basin, where permafrost thaw associated slumping has rapidly expanded in size and frequency, sediment transport across the terrestrial-aquatic continuum continues to be assessed to understand its impact on adjacent water quality and aquatic ecosystems (Kokelj et al. 2013; seeSection 3.1.4).

Sediment diagenesis encompasses the physical, chemical, and biological processes that alter the sediment properties after deposition and eventual burial. Particularly relevant for river systems are those early processes involving the rapid modification of minerals, organics, and other compounds through microbial activity, inclusive of mineral dissolution and biodegradation of organic matter. The interplay of changes within both the water column and sediment creates a complex cycle of redox driven processes that are difficult to predict. Katsev et al. (2007) studied the effects of oxygen depletion on the sediment diagenesis processes in the lower St. Lawrence River estuary, noting the increasing flux of reduced metals into the overlying water. Though comparisons between measured and modeled/predicted fluxes were similar, accurate modeling of such complex processes is difficult, especially given lack of understanding of how bioturbation and bioirrigation impact these changing benthic oxygen conditions. As dissolved oxygen (DO) conditions change at the sediment-water interface (SWI), it is difficult to understand how benthic community composition and activity will adapt, ultimately impacting the solute transport across the SWI (Katsev et al. 2007). At an ecosystem level, all these confounding processes ultimately impact the metabolic state of a system, inevitably creating a drawdown of oxygen from the water column unless supplied elsewhere. The production of reduced metals, hydrogen sulfide and methane, for example, all arise from the complex syntrophy of anaerobic processes governed by microbial activity in sediments. The importance of understanding these multi-disciplinary, syntrophic processes is vital to more holistically understanding the role of sediment diagenesis on overlying water quality in rivers and streams, and other freshwater systems.

Sediments remain an understudied aspect of process-based freshwater research, though they are integral to the cycling of organic matter, driving aquatic nutrient flux, and contribute to the overall sustainability of aquatic systems. As such, research moving forward is well suited to rely on advancements of genomics technologies to understand the concomitant roles of particulates, chemistry and microbes in the processes that control freshwater quality.

#### 3.1.4. Permafrost thaw

Permafrost thaw throughout Canada’s north is occurring at large geographic scales due to rising air temperature, but regionally may be driven by a multitude of factors such as intensifying wildfires (Gibson et al. 2018), human disturbance, changing snow cover, shrub expansion (Wilcox et al. 2019), and range expansion of ecosystem engineers (i.e., river alterations by beavers; Tape et al. 2018; Jones et al. 2020). Though permafrost thaw may be considered a total watershed process, the results of permafrost thaw are far reaching and can include altering the connectivity of inland waters, streamflow seasonality, and thaw-activated groundwater flow and associated changes to river biogeochemistry and carbon cycling (Walvoord and Kurylyk 2016). Permafrost thaw both leads to and can be mitigated or amplified by northern vegetation change (Heijmans et al. 2022), which alters downstream hydrology and water quality through changing carbon dynamics and nutrient cycling (Mekonnen et al. 2021). Indeed, some recent work demonstrates permafrost thaw is unlocking vast pools of organic carbon in northern soils (Wauthy et al. 2018), with this shift toward increasing dominance by land-derived organic carbon predicted to alter metabolic pathways and aquatic food webs. This may result in a shift toward higher methane and carbon dioxide emissions (Roiha et al. 2015). The influence of permafrost thaw on hydrology and the soil layer will have implications for release, transport and fate of nutrients, heavy metals, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) (Vonk et al. 2015). An increase in nutrient availability in freshwater could enhance algal and plant productivity in some freshwater ecosystems, leading to eutrophication risks that alter species richness and food web interactions (Wrona et al. 2016).

### 3.2. Biogeochemical processes

#### 3.2.1. Dissolved oxygen and river metabolism

DO is a key water quality parameter that is used as an indicator of the overall health of an aquatic ecosystem. It is required for the survival, growth, and reproduction of aquatic invertebrates and fishes. Reductions in the concentration of riverine DO can have detrimental consequences for aquatic organisms, including reduced health, increased incidence of deformities and reduced survival of early-life stages, increased egg incubation times, and even death (Giles and Van der Zweep 1996; Chambers et al. 2000). DO in rivers is produced as a by-product of in-river photosynthesis and from gas exchange with oxygen in the atmosphere. Oxygen be transported into the sediments through the roots of some aquatic plants, thereby influencing sediment redox conditions and the biogeochemical reactions taking place there (Pedersen et al. 2013). Aquatic photosynthesis is typically measured as gross primary productivity (GPP), which is defined as the total amount of carbon dioxide fixed by plants and algae per unit time. GPP can also be inferred from diel variation in DO concentrations as net ecosystem production (Hall and Hotchkiss 2017).

The main processes that consume DO in rivers are the chemical oxidation of compounds (chemical oxygen demand, COD), microbial-mediated oxidation of compounds (biochemical oxygen demand, BOD), and respiration by aquatic plants and animals (CCME 1999). Anthropogenic activities that impact rivers tend to increase riverine COD and BOD by increasing the availability of oxidizable compounds (e.g., dissolved organic matter (DOM), ammonium) that consume DO (Chambers et al. 1997). The balance between photosynthesis and respiration, referred to as river metabolism, along with gas exchange with the atmosphere, are important factors with respect to determining whether a river is a net source or sink of CO 2. Since all three of these processes impact DO concentrations, riverine diel DO cycles can be used to measure river metabolism (Jarvie et al. 2022).

Much of the fundamental scientific research on the processes of aquatic photosynthesis (P) and respiration (R) was done decades ago. Historically, Canadian government and academic scientists have contributed to a better process-level understanding of DO in rivers through research that has focused on subjects such as the impact of pulp mill and municipal wastewater treatment effluents and under-ice DO dynamics (Schreier et al. 1980; Chambers et al. 1997, 2000, 2006; Wassenaar et al. 2010; Culp et al. 2017; GoC 2024 _a_, 2024 _b_). Currently, Canadian research and modeling related to P and R is largely driven by the need to understand and predict DO concentrations in rivers, since these have a direct impact on the health of aquatic fauna. For example, an active topic with respect to respiration is investigation of the factors that influence the in-transit degradation of riverine organic matter (Voss et al. 2022). The impact of nutrients on algal and macrophyte growth (Standen et al. 2018) is also an active area of research related to river metabolism, both within government and academic organizations, especially as it relates to nutrients derived from agricultural activities and domestic wastewater effluent discharges (Pearce et al. 2020; Painter et al. 2021; Jarvie et al. 2022).

#### 3.2.2. Nutrient cycling and eutrophication

Inorganic nutrients, such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and silica provide chemical building blocks for life in aquatic systems. The ongoing transformations and cycling of these nutrients in aquatic systems are complex and contribute to the natural biogeochemical processes and ecosystem services these environments provide. The biogeochemistry of aquatic systems—the complex physical, chemical, and biological process interactions—are crucial to ecosystem services, controlling the degradation of organics, the cycling and production/consumption of greenhouse gases, and the overall water quality of a system. However, excess nutrients can accelerate biological activity (primary productivity), ultimately degrading water quality, contributing to eutrophication (Lund 1972). The increasing concentration of these nutrients and their impacts on freshwater rivers in Canada are a major area of research focus, especially in systems adjacent to urbanization, wastewater treatment, and agricultural land use (i.e., Chambers et al. 2008; Venkiteswaran et al. 2015; Nelligan et al. 2021). Symptoms of eutrophication include algal blooms, reduced water clarity, and oxygen depletion (hypoxia/anoxia) leading to impaired water quality ultimately impairing higher trophic level organisms (Pollock et al. 2007). The trophic state of a river/waterbody is largely controlled by nutrient loading from point and nonpoint sources, climatological conditions (such as sunlight, air temperature, precipitation, and water inflow rates), and the characteristics of the waterbody (such as depth, volume, and surface area).

The ongoing issues of eutrophication and associated harmful algal bloom development requires developing a greater and more holistic understanding of the transformations and fate of nutrients in aquatic systems. The complex interaction of fine particulates, changing redox and oxygen characteristics and dynamic biological metabolisms all coalesce to change the way nutrients are released or sequestered depending on the environmental conditions. These often-confounding processes necessitate greater understanding toward a predictive capacity to better characterize trophic energy transfer across multiple trophic levels.

#### 3.2.3. Dissolved organic matter and greenhouse gas emissions

DOM, part of the natural pool of organic matter derived from dead and decaying plant/organic biomass, has a direct impact on the biotic and abiotic processes governing freshwater quality. The most dominant constituents in DOM are carbon and oxygen, but it can also be composed of a wide-ranging diversity of nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, iron, and bind contaminants such as mercury. Derived from both terrestrial (allochthonous) and aquatic (autochthonous) sources, DOM alters the attenuation of light into the water column (Schindler et al. 1996), changes the way carbon and other nutrients are cycled and mobilized, metals and contaminants are transported, and ultimately is an integral part of microbial metabolic processes and food web dynamics (Biddanda and Cotner 2002). The interplay of DOM and the impacts/effects on the physical, chemical, and biological nature of aquatic systems makes it an integral area of focus for riverine freshwater quality alongside global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Rivers play an integral role in DOM dynamics, in their role as the primary conduit from terrestrial landscape to the receiving waters of lakes, reservoirs, and coastal oceans. Degradation of DOM through biotic and abiotic processes further alters the biogeochemical characteristics of waters and sediments, eventually impacting downstream waters. Carbon flux through these in-stream processes and subsequent downstream export are critical conduits for C flux/emissions among the larger watershed (Biddanda and Cotner 2002; Aufdenkampe et al. 2011). Importantly, DOM plays a crucial role in global climate and carbon cycles, and as such requires considerable attention to improve our understanding of its role in the physical–biogeochemical and ecological processes in rivers.

GHG budgets of surface water bodies also remain difficult to quantitatively characterize, given the complexities that surround their source/sink dynamics, and the complex processes involving DOM transformations and the gas exchange between air, water, and sediments. Inland waters have received relatively little attention in terms of their contributions to global GHG emissions, especially from “bottom-up” methodologies due to the inherent data limitations to model such processes. Despite large spatial and temporal variations in C flux among rivers, wetlands, and lakes, it is understood that rivers and streams generally account for substantial aquatic-atmospheric carbon exchange regardless of their relatively small surface area (de Melo et al. 2023). Understanding the differential drivers and dynamics of CO 2 and CH 4 emissions in these fluvial systems will be necessary to account for C source/sink dynamics on a global scale, especially in northern boreal regions facing the increasing pressures of climate change (Campeau and del Giorgio 2014). Nitrogen is even more understudied in a fluvial GHG context, though its cycling through aquatic systems is integral to biological processes and is central to microbial metabolism and overall water quality. With a range of both natural and anthropogenic sources, in excess, N can be biologically emitted from a system as nitrous oxide (N 2 O) (second only to methane in GHG potency), and as such requires improved process-based research to better define the role of rivers in the source/sink dynamics of atmospheric N at a global scale. It is estimated that globally, rivers produce approximately 20% of the estimated aquatic N 2 O emissions per year, of which 95% is anthropogenically derived (Seitzinger et al. 2000). Driven by microbial metabolism, the interplay of various physical, chemical, and biological processes has profound impacts on how important nutrients such as nitrogen and carbon are cycled, ultimately dictating whether there is a net flux of GHG(s) from a given system. Given the significant impact of climate change on the water cycle itself, naturally the flux of these GHGs will inevitably respond in tandem, especially in regions most impacted by the pressures of climate change (i.e., northern temperate and polar regions).

#### 3.2.4. Micropollutants and organic contaminants

The transport and fate of organic contaminants (i.e., polycyclic aromatic compounds (PACs), persistent organic pollutants (POPs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), pesticides, surfactant residues, microplastics, etc.) in freshwater systems is a pertinent issue with respect to point and nonpoint source agricultural, wastewater, and urban land-use practices. Their presence even in minimal concentrations can cause significant harm and adverse effects to the respective ecosystem. Organic contaminants of concern are often highly recalcitrant and thus are persistent, long-lasting pollutants in the environment. When hydrophobic in nature, they mostly associate strongly to sediments and organic matter, creating reservoirs or sinks of contaminants within the sediment compartment. By better understanding how, where, and when sediments are eroded, transported, and deposited in aquatic systems, researchers can better characterize and predict where potential contaminants can be transported and (or) sequestered.

Metals are specific conservative (nondecaying) elements that can be transformed into various forms through either complexation, adsorption, or precipitation. The fate of trace metals in a water system is determined primarily by redox and pH that influence their form and partitioning to water or to particulate matter (including phytoplankton), and by subsequent transport. The partitioning divides the total amount of a metal into a “dissolved” fraction and several “adsorbed” fractions. Both the adsorbed and dissolved fractions increase in total concentration if no solubility product is exceeded, and when it is, precipitation occurs. The fractions of a metal that are adsorbed onto particulate matter are influenced by all the processes that affect particulate matter, such as settling and resuspension.

### 3.3. Water quality indicators

Biological indicators of water quality in streams, rivers, and wetlands are of equal importance to physical or chemical indicators. Indeed, they are integral to defining a specific facet of what “quality” river water is—e.g., the capacity of the river system and water to support healthy life cycles of various organisms. Significant efforts have been undertaken in recent years to standardize the collection of this type of data, harmonize existing data, and make it open access. For instance, the Canadian Aquatic Biomonitoring Network (CABIN) is a nationally recognized, community-led program focused on assessing freshwater ecosystems and currently includes standardized protocols for wadeable streams and wetlands (CABIN 2023). The primary focus of CABIN is on monitoring benthic macroinvertebrate assemblages; data are collected concurrently with water chemistry, velocity, discharge, and habitat measurements collected through field and geospatial data. This type of biomonitoring program produces datasets based on single point or visits samplings with the understanding that the detected taxa integrate the effects of ecological habitat and water quality parameters. Covariate analysis of these data produces a “snapshot” in time, and thus are limited to providing description of temporal trends at a regional level, even with excellent spatial coverage.

Nonetheless, this type of biotic and environmental data, such as the data collected in CABIN, is complementary to and wholly necessary to national scale water quality modeling activities because it can provide necessary process-based understanding and measurements needed to refine and establish confidence in model outputs. Within CABIN, study sites are designated as reference (minimally impacted), or test (impacted) based on knowledge of the site and upstream catchment information. Currently, there are>15 000 samples collected across>12 000 sites in the database, with more added each year. However, sample distribution is both spatially and temporally limited with sample collection strongly associated with populated areas. There is significant spatial paucity for more remote regions in Canada, including much of the Arctic, and sites are often only visited once. In addition, depending on research program objectives, taxonomic identification may not be consistent or sufficient for downstream research needs.

Existing CABIN approaches are based on microscopy for sample identification but a new eDNA project is expanding taxonomic capacity through the Sequencing the Rivers for Environmental Assessment and Monitoring (STREAM) project (Robinson et al. 2021; STREAM 2023). STREAM is supported by Genome Canada and represents a collaboration among Centre for Biodiversity Genomics at University of Guelph, WWF-Canada, Living Lakes Canada, and ECCC. The STREAM method involves a modified standardized CABIN benthic macroinvertebrate sample that then uses eDNA to support more detailed biodiversity assessments, with additional markers for vertebrates (fish) recently added. To date, over 1400 samples have been collected through the STREAM project supporting wide-ranging community-based monitoring projects across Canada. These programs are but few examples of various other programs across Canada that routinely monitor the quality and characterize other riverine ecological or biological parameters (i.e., beavers, fish, mollusks, biofilms, chlorophyll a, etc.).

Similarly, the Genomics Research Development Initiative’s (GRDI’s; GRDI 2023) Ecobiomics Project is a federal initiative applying metagenomics to assess soil and aquatic biological health, and water quality. The primary focus of the aquatic portion of the network standardizes and integrates metagenomic analysis of microbial and invertebrate communities across a government-wide platform (Edge et al. 2020). Current iterations of the GRDI program include the Genomic Adaptation and Resilience to Climate Change, which employs genomics approaches to assess biological health and stability across Canadian environments in the face of climate change effects. Further, GRDI Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) uses genomics’ approaches to monitor and understand emergence and transmission of human pathogens and AMR in Canadian aquatic environments, and the influence of various contaminants on these dynamics, among other objectives. These research programs are identified as being direct down-stream users of outputs from the proposed NWQMF, to provide more fulsome environmental context for their genomics-based conclusions and predictions.

### 3.4. Functional (ecological) indicators and processes

River ecological processes are wide ranging and inherently complex given the interconnectedness of ecological structure and functions. These ecological and associated governing biogeochemical processes are the critical connection between abiotic and biotic components, are directly impacted by water quality, but can also provide insight into the status of water quality. Functional indicators are biological or biochemical parameters or processes that function to summarize complex information about ecosystem state or “health”, particularly in response to perturbations (Niemeijer and de Groot 2008; Müller et al. 2013; Bonilla-Valencia et al. 2022). These indicators provide the direct connection between water quality and the provision of ecosystem services, resilience of ecosystems to disturbance, and shifting biodiversity patterns (i.e., food web structure, taxonomic diversity). Historically, assessment of species richness could indicate or give insight into ecosystem structure and overall ecosystem services. Specific organisms or taxa that share similar attributes or impact ecosystem processes in parallel ways therefore serve as a “functional group” (Bonsdorff and Pearson 1999). Alongside increased concern for biodiversity, there has been an expansion in the range of indicators of interest to include functional diversity metrics such as biological traits, which are the morphological (e.g., size, body form), physiological (e.g., mobility, feeding mode, temperature tolerances), behavioral (e.g., bioturbation), and phenological (e.g., life span, maturity) traits of a given species (Tilman et al. 1997; Díaz and Cabido 2001; Song et al. 2014). The interaction of these functional traits directly impacts ecosystem function (e.g., nutrient recycling, production, sediment stability, habitat structure, etc.) and thus the stability of the overall community (Loreau et al. 2001).

Functional indicators can also include ecological processes that are mediated by biotic communities (e.g., microbial decomposers and shredder macroinvertebrates) and are highly sensitive to changes in water quality. Organic matter decomposition is an ecological process at the base of aquatic food webs that connects terrestrial vegetation (e.g., riparian forests) to aquatic communities through the cycling of nutrients. This process underpins many freshwater ecosystems and provides energy through bottom-up interactions in food webs to higher trophic levels such as fish. Given that this process connects multiple levels of biotic organization and is critical to energy cycling, rates of organic matter processing are highly sensitive measures of ecological integrity. There are well-developed techniques to measure organic matter decomposition and associated biodiversity and recent publications reflect the global importance of this functional indicator to carbon cycling feedback and for sustaining freshwater biota (Tiegs et al. 2019; Costello et al. 2022).

Knowledge of functional trait interactions can aid in the prediction of community response to various environmental stresses (Lavore and Garnier 2002). By increasing the number of traits examined, there is potential to reveal greater functional diversity following adverse environmental conditions (i.e., contamination), than would be gleaned from solely examining species richness (Ghilarov 2000). In turn, characterization of functional trait response(s) to conditions, produces stronger mechanistic understanding of various ecosystem services and their relationship with environmental stress. The field of “omics” is a very promising and data-dense means of understanding these mechanisms. Approaches such as (meta)genomics, (meta)transcriptomics, metabolomics, (meta)proteomics, (meta)lipidomics, allow for the characterization and quantification of the total gene, gene transcript, metabolite, protein, and lipid content, respectively, of a given sample. Understanding specific gene or metabolite “signatures” of environmental conditions can assist in describing and assessing broader ecosystem functions (Pomfret et al. 2020; Cohen et al. 2022). Importantly, these techniques can be applied to a specific environmental matrix (i.e., sediment, water, biofilms) to assess microbial function (Falk et al. 2019; Bergsveinson et al. 2020; Reid et al. 2020) or to a targeted tissue type of a higher order organism (i.e., invertebrates, fish) (Fernández-Cisnal et al. 2018; Izral et al. 2021; Brua et al. 2022). Ultimately, these approaches reveal unique “marker” genes or compounds that correspond to specific functional traits of a community or organism. Importantly, the use of these techniques to assess and develop functional trait markers is in its relative infancy, as compared to invertebrate taxonomic classification and study. Furthermore, there are considerable technical considerations and limitations that must be weighed to ensure the data serve the goal of a given study (Lankadurai et al. 2013; Shakya et al. 2019; Dumas et al. 2022; Thukral et al. 2023).

## 4. River water quality modeling

It is evident from analysis of processes above that water quality management requires the collection and analysis of large and diverse datasets, which can be difficult to evaluate and synthesize, particularly over space and time. As previously mentioned, tools such as the CCME WQI (Saffran et al. 2001) have been developed and are currently in use that intend to integrate some of these parameters to provide an assessment of a given water bodies suitability to support aquatic life and human activities in specific monitoring sites in Canada (Paun et al. 2016). However, for the purposes of developing a holistic and predictive NWQMS, WQI models cannot easily simulate cause–effect relationships between pollutant loadings and the receiving waterbody and (or) estimate the potential impacts of contaminant and nutrient loads from human activity, new management strategies, or a changing climate. To achieve those aims, either empirical or mechanistic models must be developed to describe and account for the various parameters of interest. A generic water quality model of a river system can be defined as a mathematical model that computes the quality of a receiving water as a function of internal loading and effluent release to the system. Such model can be represented generally as:

![Image 5](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq1.gif)

(1)

where _W_ [M T−1] is input load into the river (in mass (M) per unit time (T−1)) and _C_ [M L−3] is the resulting concentration of a specific constituent in the river (in mass (M) per unit volume (L−3)). The above equation indicates that the cause–effect relationship between load and concentration depends on the physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of the effluent and receiving water. Such models can be implemented in simulation mode to compute the system response (i.e., concentration) as a function of the loading and system characteristics, or in design mode to compute the loading required to meet a desired concentration level (Chapra 2008).

### 4.1. Empirical versus mechanistic models

Empirical models are based on an inductive or data-based approach, which involves collecting values of _W_ and _C_ at various times or from many similar systems and employing regression techniques to statistically simulate the dependencies. In recent years, various nonlinear models such as artificial neural network (ANN), Random Forest Decision Tree (RFDT), and support vector machine among others have been used for the prediction of water quality variables (Khullar and Singh 2021). A limitation of empirical models is that they are conditioned on historical observations, and as such, their predictive capability assumes conditions like those in the observational record. To simulate previously unrecorded extreme conditions from this model would entail extrapolating potentially unreliably beyond the range of variables on which the model was built (de la Mare et al. 2012). Mechanistic models on the other hand are based on deductive approaches involving the use of theoretical relationships or organizing principles. Most mechanistic water-quality models are based on conservation of mass that can be expressed as a mass balance equation that accounts for all transfers of matter across the system’s boundaries, and for all transformations occurring within the system. For a finite period, this can be generally expressed as:

![Image 6](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq2.gif)

(2)

By combining all the factors in equation form, the mass balance represents a bookkeeping exercise for the constituent being modeled. Hence, the mathematical expression of mass conservation provides a framework for calculating the response of a body of water to external influences (Chapra 2008). Over time, surface water quality models have progressed from considering a single water quality parameter to multi-parameters, from steady-state to dynamic models, from point source modeling to the coupling of point and nonpoint sources, and from zero-dimensional model to one-, two-, and three-dimensional models (Wang et al. 2013). Successful river water quality modeling requires the specification of an appropriate model structure and process formulation.

#### 4.1.1. Advection–dispersion–reaction equation

Mechanistic water quality models are built based on (1) conservation of mass balance, (2) laws governing chemical, biochemical, and biological processes, and (3) boundary and initial conditions. The following conservation of mass equation accounts for the material entering/leaving the water body, transport of the material within the water body, and physical, chemical, and biological transformation of the material.

![Image 7](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq3.gif)

(3)

where _C_ is concentration of water quality state variable; _u, v_, and _w_ are velocity components in the _x, y_, and _z_ directions, respectively; _K_ x, _K_ y, and _K_ z are turbulent diffusivities in the _x, y_, and _z_ directions, respectively; and _S_ is external sources and sinks per unit volume and _f_ R is the reaction term representing conversion rates of state variables due to biological, chemical, and other conversion processes as a function of concentration. This equation incorporates transport due to flow advection and dispersion, external pollutant inputs, and the kinetic interaction between the water quality variables. The variables _u, v_, and _w_ and _K_ x, _K_ y, and _K_ z are independent of _C_ and thus may be determined externally to the water-quality model. The hydrodynamic model provides the information needed for the water quality modeling, including water depth, flow velocity, turbulent mixing, water temperature, and sediment concentration. In most practical cases, the problems of river water quality are satisfactorily approached in steady conditions, under which parameters are not changed over time.

#### 4.1.2. Kinetic processes representation

The term kinetic refers to the mathematical description of the time dependency of any dynamic process, which can be physical (e.g., sorption and atmospheric deposition), chemical (e.g., nitrification), or biochemical (e.g., algal growth and uptake). The kinetic process can be decoupled from the rest of the advection–dispersion equation and can be represented as:

![Image 8](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq4.gif)

(4)

First-order kinetics derived by linearizing _f_ R, with respect to _C_, is used in most water quality models:

![Image 9](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq5.gif)

(5)

where _k_ is kinetic rate (t−1) and _S_=source/sink term due to internal and external sources (mass/volume/time). A major task of a water quality model is to formulate _k_ and _S_ so that water quality processes can be represented realistically. Major differences between water quality models are primarily in how the kinetic equation is specified, how many nutrients are simulated, and how many state variables are included to describe each nutrient cycle. Empirical formulations are often used as an approximation for specifying the model parameters (_k_ and _S_). For example, most water quality processes are temperature dependent, hence the kinetic rate _k_ is linked to the water temperature as follows:

![Image 10](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq6.gif)

(6)

where _k_ 20 is the kinetic rate at 20°C and _θ_ is the temperature effect constant, which usually has a value slightly greater than 1.

The above is a generic description of water quality models used to predict or describe water quality parameters over time and through space. In the following sections (Sections 4.2–4.8), we describe the state of the models used to account for key variables outlined in Section 3.

### 4.2. Water temperature and river ice modeling

Several approaches are available for modeling water temperature in river systems with the main two being: (i) deterministic models that use process-based equations to consider energy budget and heat exchange in water bodies and (ii) statistical or stochastic models that rely on relations of water temperature with driving variables (Ouellet et al. 2020). While deterministic models are data, resource, and time intensive to set up and calibrate, they arguably provide a credible basis for impact studies, such as predicting impacts of structures, land use, and climate change. Statistical or stochastic models have lower data/computational requirements, as they generally simulate river water temperature based on hydro-meteorological drivers (e.g., air temperature, precipitation, snow, discharge, etc.). A parametric linear regression is the simplest form of the statistical model (Benyahya et al. 2007), while nonlinear methods based on modern machine learning, such as ANN and RFDT (Gallice et al. 2015; Ouellet et al. 2020) and hybrid methods, for example, air2stream model that combine simplified empirical equations with statistical methods (Toffolon and Piccolroaz 2015) are becoming more common. However, the statistical and empirical models may be less reliable in simulating future climate responses compared to deterministic models (Arismendi et al. 2014; Leach and Moore 2019; Lee et al. 2020; Shrestha and Pesklevits 2023 _a_).

The effect of ice cover on boundary shear stresses/velocity field, and thence on the mixing capacity of the river, can easily be modeled and predictions made after experimental assessment of transverse or longitudinal dispersion coefficients. Since most river ice phenomena are governed by thermal and ice transport, along with mechanical and thermal processes and phase changes, a coherent river ice model can be formulated with a thermal-ice transport framework encompassing river ice evolution from freezeup to breakup (Shen 2010; Blackburn and She 2019).

### 4.3. Sediment transport and diagenesis modeling

From a water quality perspective, the most important sediment processes are erosion/resuspension, transportation, and deposition of sediments. Sediment erosion (_S_ e) and deposition (_S_ d) are source and sink terms in the advection–dispersion equation. The riverbed will erode, and resuspension initiated when the bed shear stress, _τ_ b, exceeds a critical shear stress for erosion, _τ_ ce. Deposition of suspended sediment particles and flocs occurs when the mean flow velocity is sufficiently low so that the corresponding bed shear stress, _τ_ b, is less than the critical shear stress for deposition, _τ_ cd, that would result in the particles and flocs falling to the bed and remaining there. The deposition and erosion rates _S_ d, _S_ e [ML−2 T−1] can be expressed by Van Rijn (1984):

![Image 11](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq7.gif)

(7)

![Image 12](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq8.gif)

(8)

where _W_ s is settling velocity of sediment particles, _c_ is near bed sediment concentration, and _E_ 0 and _n_ are the erosion coefficient and exponent, respectively. The local bed shear stress can be given by:

![Image 13](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq9.gif)

(9)

where _C_ ch is the Chezy resistance number, _h_ is the flow depth, _n_ is Manning’s number, and _V_ is the flow velocity. Many empirical formulas have been proposed for estimating the settling velocity of sediments (_W_ s); however, in most models, _W_ s is often used as a calibration parameter to fit measured sediment data (Ji 2008).

Following the deposition and subsequent burial of sediments, chemical interactions between the bed sediment and water column and (or) pore water are key components of aquatic biogeochemistry and ecology. The microbial oxidation of organic matter is one of the major processes driving chemical changes in stream bed sediment. Sediment diagenesis models parameterize and combine transport processes and reaction pathways to explore the system responses of the sediment layer. The modeling of organic matter mineralization defines the reaction rate to be proportional to the organic matter concentration, rather than the oxidant concentration, thereby assuming that organic matter availability was the primary control on the mineralization rate. Therefore, a general diagenetic equation is defined as the sum of chemical reactions and physical processes—advection, diffusion, and biological mixing (Paraska et al. 2014):

![Image 14](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq10.gif)

(10)

![Image 15](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq11.gif)

(11)

where _R_ s is a generic reaction term identifier that applies to the solid substance reactions and _R_ d to dissolved substance reactions, _C_ s is a species’ concentration, _ρ_ is sediment density, _t_ is time, _D_ B is the biodiffusion coefficient, _D_ S is the molecular diffusion coefficient, _x_ is depth, ϕ is porosity, _ω_ is the rate of burial, _v_ is the velocity of flow relative to the sediment surface, α is an irrigation constant, and _C_ d0 is the concentration of a dissolved substance at the SWI.

### 4.4. Dissolved oxygen (DO) and river metabolism modeling

There are multiple interconnected processes controlling river DO concentration, thus process-based models that consider all factors carry inherent uncertainty and require extensive calibration. These processes include the production of oxygen from gross primary production (GPP; river metabolism); oxygen depletion from the process of autotrophic respiration, assimilation of oxygen during nitrification, benthic respiration (i.e., sediment oxygen demand), and biological respiration within the water column (i.e., BOD); oxygen exchange via reaeration; and DO advection/transformation. In shallower and stony bottomed streams and rivers, features of velocity, reaeration, and benthic primary production and respiration are the dominant terms controlling DO and metabolism. These processes are further influenced by hydrology, biogeochemistry, altitude, and temperature. Given the interplay of chemical and biological functions, multiple key variables must be incorporated into any model, including water temperature, DO, nitrate and ammonium, particulate organic nitrogen, organic and inorganic phosphorus, BOD, photosynthetically active radiation, and chlorophyll _a_ (Chl _a_); each of which are accounted for and incorporated via specific equations. The most generalized, process-based relationship accounting for DO advection, GPP and ecosystem respiration, and reaeration is (Pathak et al. 2022):

![Image 16](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq12.gif)

(12)

where _C_ DO,_i_ and _C_ DO,_o_ are the input and output DO concentration (mg·L−1) across a river reach, respectively; _W_ is the aeration at weirs (mg O 2 L−1); _P_ GPP is the GPP (mg O 2 L−1 h−1); _R_ ER is the ecosystem respiration (mg O 2 L−1 h−1), and _F_ is aeration at the air–water surface (mg O 2 L−1 h−1) (Pathak et al. 2022).

The rate of oxygen production (_P_ GPP) and oxygen depletion (_R_ ER) are further represented, respectively, by:

![Image 17](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq13.gif)

(13)

![Image 18](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq14.gif)

(14)

where _P_ P is oxygen production from photosynthesis and _P_ N is the oxygen produced during nitrate assimilation by biomass; _R_ A is the autotrophic respiration; a function of phytoplankton respiration rate and temperature; _R_ nitri is the assimilation of oxygen in the process of nitrification of ammonium to nitrate; _R_ ben is the sediment oxygen demand (benthic respiration); and _R_ wc is water column BOD (all terms as mg O 2 L−1 h−1) (Pathak et al. 2022). Given the incorporation of phytoplankton respiration and sediment oxygen demand, this model or relationships would be most representative of lowland rivers.

### 4.5. Nutrients and eutrophication modeling

The most widely used variables to describe eutrophication are total phosphorus, total nitrogen, and chlorophyll. Other variables such as DO are also useful indicators of the eutrophication status of a water body. Hydrodynamic processes in a river control the transport of nutrients and algae, and phosphorus and nitrogen can attach to sediments in water, and the sorption and desorption process affects the nutrient transport and uptake in the water system (Fig. 1; Chapra 2008). Algae and phytoplankton (deeper rivers) or periphyton (shallow, stony rivers or streams) play a key role in the eutrophication process as they affect the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, the DO balance, and the aquatic food chain, primarily through nutrient uptake and algal growth and death. Algal growth rate is controlled by temperature, water movement, nutrients, and light. The Michaelis–Menten formulation is widely used to represent the rate of algal growth as follows (Ji 2017):

![Image 19](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq15.gif)

(15)

where _k_ C is algal growth rate (1/time), _k_ max is maximum algal growth rate (1/time), and _C_ is nutrient concentration (mg·L–1 or moles), and _C_ H is half-saturation concentration (mg·L–1), which is the nutrient concentration at which the growth rate is one-half of the maximum rate.

Fig. 1.

![Image 20](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_f1.jpg)

Fig. 1. Processes involved in nutrient and aquatic biota kinetics (adapted from Mao et al. 2015). Red text indicates the varied processes that must occur to transfer or transform nutrients within and between river compartments.

Nitrogen and phosphorus are required by all algal species, while silica is required by only diatoms. Liebig’s law of the minimum indicates that algal growth is controlled by nutrient in least supply (Ji 2017). With more than one nutrient accounted for, the algal growth rate can be calculated by:

![Image 21](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq16.gif)

(16)

where _C_ N, P, Si=concentrations of available inorganic N, orthophosphate, and available silica, and _C_ HN, P, Si=half saturation concentrations of N, P, and Si.

### 4.6. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) and greenhouse gases (GHG)

To understand and predict the complex dynamics of organic matter in soils and surface waters, process-based biogeochemical models are required. This remains a challenge, as it is difficult to represent and integrate all the necessary processes to model DOM at a scale greater than an individual catchment over annual to decadal timescales. Specifically, for dissolved organic carbon (DOC), a process-based biogeochemical model should: (1) incorporate spatial heterogeneity and land use, (2) simulate effects of changing precipitation patterns and temperature, (3) account for in-soil production and consumption of organic material, (4) quantify surface water fluxes of DOC, and (5) represent the biological and chemical processes that consume DOC (Futter et al. 2007). Additionally, models require the ability to be parameterized and calibrated with routine monitoring data.

Modeling efforts to forecast DOM require a detailed understanding and representation of the pool sizes of litter and humus (i.e., high microbial activity, high fungal abundance, and conditions that enhance mineralization may promote high DOM concentrations) as well as the hydrologic variability across time and space to mobilize and potentially transform these pools (Kalbitz et al. 2000). Modeling of DOM cycling also requires an understanding of terrigenous and autochthonous DOM. Terrigenous DOM is divided into T 1 (strongly UV absorbing) and T 2 (non- or weakly UV absorbing) fractions that differ in responses to microbial consumption, photooxidation, and flocculation. These can be distinguished through measurements based on specific UV absorbance that are widespread in observational field data. Autochthonous DOM is produced in situ through processes including phytoplankton or periphytic exudation, zooplankton or zoobenthic grazing, and detritus turnover, and comprises a spectrum of compounds of varying lability. Linked to DOM are processes described in Section 4.3. Sediment Transport and Diagenesis Modeling, including the converse role of pelagic processes (phytoplankton and algae) versus benthic processes in headwater streams and midreach rivers. UniDOM is an example of a fully functional model that represents the bulk DOC pool that can be linked to soil models to generate input fluxes of terrigenous DOM and was developed using data from the boreal northern hemisphere (Anderson et al. 2019).

Linked to modeling of DOC and DOM is the globally important field of modeling GHG sources, emissions, and cycling in terrestrial and freshwater bodies. Given rivers and other inland waterbodies receive considerable amounts of reactive organic matter from the terrestrial environment, they are net-sources for GHG’s such as CO 2, CH 4, and N 2 O. Once more, multiple processes govern GHG production in rivers, which include terrestrial and wetland run-off, respiration (microbial and plant), the reducing and oxidizing conditions at the interface between surface and subsurface zones, and the influence of nitrification/denitrification and methanogenesis (Marzadri et al. 2017, 2021; DelSontro et al. 2018; Abril and Borges 2019). These processes are complex and thus there are large uncertainties related to modeling GHG production and cycling from inland waters at large scale. One such initiative, the Regional Carbon Cycle Assessment and Processes Phase 1 (RECCAP1; Canadell et al. 2011; Lauerwald et al. 2023 _a_), took aim to establish global CO 2 budgets across large regions (continent-sized). The second phase (RECCAP2) considers CO 2, CH 4, and N 2 O. Generally, these large-scale estimates of inland water GHG emissions (_F_ GHG) are calculated as the product of an average flux rate, _f_ GHG, (units of mass per area and time; derived from field observations) and the estimate of inland water surface area, _A_ IW:

![Image 22](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq17.gif)

(17)

These global assessments have been used to derive a regionalized assessment for 10 extensive land regions used in RECCAP2 (Lauerwald et al. 2023 _a_, 2023 _b_), that also corrected for the effects of seasonal ice cover. These findings indicate rivers to be the largest CO 2 emitters over a 100-year time horizon, thus providing strong impetus for gathering further empirical measurements and the development of robust, process-based models of riverine GHG emissions within Canada and internationally that include small and ephemeral river bodies.

### 4.7. Micropollutant and organic contaminants modeling

Micro-pollutants are substances that at low concentrations can impair the reproduction and growth of organisms, including fish and human beings (Loucks and van Beek 2017). These substances include trace metals, many synthetic organic compounds (organic micro-pollutants), and radioactive substances. Metals are conservative (nondecaying) substances that can be transformed into various species through either complexation, adsorption, redox reaction, or precipitation. Organic micro-pollutants are lost by volatilization, biodegradation, photolysis, hydrolysis, and overall degradation. Most of these processes are usually modeled as first-order processes, with associated rate constants that are temperature dependent. To model the transport and fate of micro-pollutants, the adsorption–desorption process, estimate of the suspended sediment concentration, settling and resuspension from the bottom are required (Ji 2017). The adsorption–desorption model assumes that an equilibrium exists between the dissolved (in water) and adsorbed (on sediments) concentrations of a constituent such as a heavy metal or organic contaminant (Fig. 2). This equilibrium follows a linear relationship, with its slope being the partition coefficient _k_ p (L·kg–1). Each partition coefficient _k_ p is defined as the ratio of the particulate concentration _C_ p of a micro-pollutant (mg·kg–1) divided by the dissolved concentration _C_ d of a micro-pollutant (mg·L–1).

![Image 23](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_eq18.gif)

(18)

Fig. 2.

![Image 24](https://cdnsciencepub.com/cms/10.1139/er-2023-0094/asset/images/er-2023-0094_f2.jpg)

Fig. 2. Adsorption–desorption model of fate and transport processes for micro-pollutants within a river system (adapted from Ji 2008).

The presence of a micro-pollutant in a water system is described by the total concentration (sum of dissolved and particulate concentrations) for each water and sediment compartment. Because the fate of most micro-pollutants is largely determined by adsorption to particulate matter, suspended inorganic and organic matter (including phytoplankton) must be included in the model and it may also be necessary to include DOM as well (Chapra 2008). The adsorbed fractions in the water column are subject to settling and the fractions in the sediment are subject to resuspension. The rates of settling and resuspension of micro-pollutants are therefore proportional to the rates for particulate matter. The adsorbed fractions in the sediment can also be removed from the water system by deposition/burial. An additional process called bioturbation, caused by the physical activity of organisms that leads to the redistribution of the micro-pollutant among sediment layers, is considered by means of dispersion coefficients (Loucks and van Beek 2017).

### 4.8. Ecological modeling

#### 4.8.1. Dependent variables (biota)

Modeling of biological and ecological dynamics is varied and highly specific to research objectives and data types. Conceptually, these models assume that local biota are reflective of the broader biophysical processes that influence the ecosystem, and that understanding distribution, diversity, and niche of biota provides insight for environmental management and predictive power into ecosystem dynamics. For instance, both species distribution models and ecological niche models are based on ecological niche theor

I'm setting up a national statistical analysis of environmental sustainability measures taken by Canadian provinces and territories. Can you give me a list of all the provinces/territories that had a decrease in greenhouse gas emissions in 2023 from 2005 by at least 15%, had at least 10% of their terrestrial area conserved in 2023, and are a part of the two river regions with the highest proportion of sites with "good" or "excellent" river water quality from the 2021 to 2023 period? Canadian rivers – Water quality at monitoring sites The Canadian Environmental Sustainability Indicators (CESI) program provides data and information to track Canada's performance on key environmental sustainability issues. The Water quality in Canadian rivers indicators provide a measure of the ability of river water across Canada to support plants and animals. At each monitoring site, water quality data are compared to water quality guidelines to create a rating for the site. If measured water quality is below the guidelines, it can maintain a healthy ecosystem. Water quality at a monitoring site is considered excellent when substances in a river are very rarely measured above their guidelines. Conversely, water quality is rated poor when measurements are usually above their guidelines, sometimes by a wide margin. These indicators provide information about the state of surface water quality and its change through time, to support water resource management. Information is provided to Canadians in a number of formats including: static and interactive maps, charts and graphs, HTML and CSV data tables and downloadable reports. See the supplementary documentation for the data sources and details on how the data were collected and how the indicator was calculated.

The Water quality in Canadian rivers indicators provide a measure of the ability of river water across Canada to support plants and animals. At each monitoring site, water quality data are compared to water quality guidelines to create a rating for the site. If measured water quality is below the guidelines, it can maintain a healthy ecosystem. Water quality at a monitoring site is considered excellent when substances in a river are very rarely measured above their guidelines. Conversely, water quality is rated poor when measurements are usually above their guidelines, sometimes by a wide margin. These indicators provide information about the state of surface water quality and its change through time, to support water resource management. Information is provided to Canadians in a number of formats including: static and interactive maps, charts and graphs, HTML and CSV data tables and downloadable reports. See the supplementary documentation for the data sources and details on how the data were collected and how the indicator was calculated. Canadian rivers – Water quality at monitoring sites The Canadian Environmental Sustainability Indicators (CESI) program provides data and information to track Canada's performance on key environmental sustainability issues. The Water quality in Canadian rivers indicators provide a measure of the ability of river water across Canada to support plants and animals. At each monitoring site, water quality data are compared to water quality guidelines to create a rating for the site. If measured water quality is below the guidelines, it can maintain a healthy ecosystem. Water quality at a monitoring site is considered excellent when substances in a river are very rarely measured above their guidelines. Conversely, water quality is rated poor when measurements are usually above their guidelines, sometimes by a wide margin. These indicators provide information about the state of surface water quality and its change through time, to support water resource management. Information is provided to Canadians in a number of formats including: static and interactive maps, charts and graphs, HTML and CSV data tables and downloadable reports. See the supplementary documentation for the data sources and details on how the data were collected and how the indicator was calculated.

## Abstract

This article presents the first comprehensive review and analysis of the uptake of the Canadian Drinking Water Quality Guidelines (CDWQG) across Canada’s 13 provinces and territories. This review is significant given that Canada’s approach to drinking water governance is: (i) highly decentralized and (ii) discretionary. Canada is (along with Australia) only one of two Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) member states that does not comply with the World Health Organization’s (WHO) recommendation that all countries have national, legally binding drinking water quality standards. Our review identifies key differences in the regulatory approaches to drinking water quality across Canada’s 13 jurisdictions. Only 16 of the 94 CDWQG are consistently applied across all 13 jurisdictions; five jurisdictions use voluntary guidelines, whereas eight use mandatory standards. The analysis explores three questions of central importance for water managers and public health officials: (i) should standards be uniform or variable; (ii) should compliance be voluntary or legally binding; and (iii) should regulation and oversight be harmonized or delegated? We conclude with recommendations for further research, with particular reference to the relevance of our findings given the high degree of variability in drinking water management and oversight capacity between urban and rural areas in Canada.

**Keywords:**drinking water guidelines, drinking water standards, decentralized water governance, water policy, heterogeneity, Canada

## 1. Introduction

Threats to drinking water across Canada and internationally have drawn attention to the importance of governance in safeguarding drinking water and public health [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]. Within this broader debate, one key issue is the allocation of responsibility for standard setting for drinking water. Drawing on a case study of Canada, this paper analyzes three issues of central importance for water managers and public health officials: (i) should standards be uniform or variable; (ii) should compliancy be voluntary or legally binding; and (iii) should regulation and oversight be harmonized or delegated? These questions are of particular interest internationally given the fact that greater decentralization and subsidiarity have been recent trends in water governance, despite the recommendation by the World Health Organization for national legally binding, uniform standards.

To address these concerns, the article presents the first comprehensive review and evaluation of the uptake and application of Canadian Drinking Water Quality Guidelines (CDWQG) across Canada’s 13 jurisdictions: 10 provinces and three territories. (Provinces and territories are very similar to American or Australian states. The main difference between provinces and territories is that the former (located in the more populous south of the country) receive power and authority directly from Canada’s Constitution Act of 1867, whereas the latter (located in the sparsely populated north of the country) are granted somewhat more limited mandates and powers from the federal government). This review is significant given Canada’s highly decentralized approach to drinking water governance. Canada is the only Group of Eight (G8) country and (along with Australia) only one of two Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) member states that does not have legally enforceable drinking water quality standards at the national level—despite “best practice” World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations [3,8]. Thus, Canada is a “natural laboratory” in which to study the questions raised above, as standards are variable across jurisdictions, regulation is characterized by a combination of harmonization and delegation, and only eight jurisdictions have decided to adopt legally binding standards, while others rely on voluntary approaches. The process of drinking water quality standard-setting in Canada reflects the country’s highly decentralized approach to water governance. Canada is unique amongst industrialized countries, notably with respect to the relatively passive role taken by the federal government in matters of drinking water regulation—in contrast to other federations, such as the USA and European Union, which have a higher degree of consistency across their respective territories, and unlike Canada, mandate legally binding, uniform drinking water quality standards.

In Canada, decentralization arises as a result of the constitutional division of powers between scales of government. As a result, water management is shared by the federal and provincial governments. The federal government’s water responsibilities include navigable waters, fisheries and transboundary waters. Canada’s ten provinces, which derive their authority from the 1867 Constitution Act, have constitutional responsibility for fresh water, natural resources, and health. The three territories (Northwest Territories, Nunavut, and Yukon), differ in that their power and mandates do not derive from the constitution, but rather are delegated under the authority of Canada’s Parliament—although the Government of Canada is increasingly transferring province-like powers to territorial governments. An attempt at harmonization of drinking water quality has been made through a non-binding federal process: the Federal-Provincial-Technical Committee on Drinking Water (FPTCDW). This federal agency, with membership from the provinces and territories, develops the Canadian Drinking Water Quality Guidelines. Since the national guidelines are voluntary and non-enforceable, Canadian jurisdictions have the autonomy to decide whether or not to adopt the CDWQG, to what extent they apply the guidelines, and whether to make them legally enforceable. In short, it is the jurisdictions that have ultimate responsibility for formulating their own drinking water standards, and ensuring that public health and related goals are met [3,9]. As a result, Canada is one of the few examples whereby drinking-water quality management is not standardized across the country. As such, two key governance issues raised by the current situation in Canada include: (i) the high degree of voluntarism and (ii) delegation of responsibility (or decentralization of authority).

What are the implications of this decentralization of governance, and associated variation in standards? What can be learned from a careful evaluation of the Canadian case in terms of the variation that this framework has produced? Both within Canada and internationally, some experts argue that greater harmonization and formal regulation (and a lower degree of voluntarism and subsidiarity) is required [10,11,12,13,14]. In contrast, others argue in favor of decentralization, advocate subsidiarity, and assert that public health protection will be improved by greater ‘system knowledge’ and contextually specific approaches, rather than formal and standardized regulations [2,15,16]. Proponents of decentralization also point to Canada’s size and geography, arguing that heterogeneity in governance may be functional (to some degree), because it permits adaptation of regulations to local biophysical conditions. However, critics have argued that that Canada’s decentralized regulatory model and nonbinding drinking water quality guidelines foster inequities, with some Canadians being protected by more stringent rules than others, particularly First Nation and rural communities [10,17,18,19,20,21]. In addition, it is argued that the decentralized approach has impacted data collection and quality, which in turn has created its own set of problems. In summary, the literature suggests that there may be both positive and negative aspects of decentralized water governance [22,23,24].

This paper contributes to these debates by providing a systematic study of variation in drinking water standards and guidelines. No prior systematic study of this topic in Canada has been published in the scholarly literature. Our research addresses this gap by compiling an inventory of drinking water quality parameters used in Canadian provinces and territories (the first of its kind); analyzing the extent of variation; identifying the baseline of drinking water parameters applied uniformly across provinces and territories, and highlighting some of the implications, for Canada and for the broader debates as noted.

## 2. Method

Data was compiled through publicly available information sources including government agency websites, reports and legislation. Each province and territory drinking water guideline/standard was compared against the 2012 Canadian Drinking Water Quality Guidelines, which is comprises of 94 chemical, physical, microbial, and radiological parameters. These parameters include health considerations (maximum acceptable concentrations (MAC)), aesthetic considerations (aesthetic objectives (AO)), and operational guideline values (operational guidance (OG)) [25].

The analysis includes five categories: (1)The province/territory uses exactly the same parameter value as the CDWQG;(2)The parameter value used by the province/territory is less stringent than the CDWQG;(3)The parameter value used by the province/territory is more stringent than the CDWQG;(4)The province/territory uses a parameter that is not listed under the CDWQG;(5)A CDWQG is not used by the province/territory;

The database was further analyzed to identify which parameters are consistently applied (at the same value) across all jurisdictions; which jurisdictions use different values for given parameters; which parameters are applied widely but not by all jurisdictions; which are the ‘outlier’ parameters, _i.e._, parameters that are only applied by one or two jurisdictions.

Three researchers re-checked all the data in the database for accuracy. The data and analysis was then sent to relevant agencies in each of the ten provinces and three territorial jurisdictions to verify the data and analysis were correct to ensure that the inventory was both comprehensive and accurate. Agency staff that reviewed the data included Provincial Health Officers, Drinking Water Officers, water quality specialists, scientists and technicians. Over 90% of the provincial agencies contacted provided feedback. All but one jurisdiction responded with comments, which were subsequently incorporated into the analysis.

## 3. Results

Guidelines, standards, codes of practice, and policies only become enforceable when they are implemented in legislation. Since the Canadian Drinking Water Quality Guidelines are voluntary non-enforceable guidelines, Canadian provinces and territories are able to choose: (i) whether or not to adopt the CDWQG; (ii) to what extent they apply the guidelines, and (iii) whether to make them legally enforceable [3].

### 3.1. Legal Approaches to Drinking Water

Eight of the 13 jurisdictions have legally binding drinking water regulations (see Table 1). However, only one of these eight jurisdictions, the Northwest Territories, has adopted all 94 CDWQG into provincial regulation. Nova Scotia and Manitoba have adopted the majority of the CDWQG into provincial regulation. The remaining five jurisdictions (Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Québec and Yukon) have partially adopted the CDWQG into legislation (see Table 2).

Whilst BC follows the CDWQG in their entirety (see Table 2), only the microbial indicators are legally binding. According to the British Columbia Water and Wastewater Association (BCWWA), BC is currently the only provincial or state level of government in North America that does not explicitly identify drinking water standards beyond bacterial indicators. Non-legally binding approaches are also taken in New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador and Nunavut.

Table 1

| Jurisdiction | Legally Binding | Comments |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| British Columbia (BC) | N | Depending on the variable in question and the nature of the water supplier there may be an absolute requirement to meet a guideline, or there may be allowances for slight elevation above the guideline, or periodic exceedance. |
| Alberta (AB) | Y | Public Health Act—Nuisance and General Sanitation Regulation (Section 11) and the Environmental Protection and Enhancement Act (EPEA). |
| Saskatchewan (SK) | Y | The Saskatchewan Standards are enforceable under The Environment Management and Protection Act, 2002 and The Water Regulations, 2002. |
| Manitoba (MB) | Y | Chemical standards are enforced under the Drinking Water Quality Standards Regulation. Manitoba adopts all other parameters either from CDWQG or CCME as general guidelines by policy. |
| Ontario (ON) | Y | Safe Drinking Water Act, Ontario Regulation 169/03—Ontario Drinking Water Quality Standards. |
